2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same notebook or project.

You will try tree-based models, compare them with cross-validation, and learn to spot overfitting by comparing training and test error. You end the week with a saved best model and a chart showing which features matter most.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Decision trees and random forests for regression
- Overfitting: when a model memorises the training data
- Comparing models fairly with cross-validation
- Feature importance and saving models with `joblib`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Train a `DecisionTreeRegressor` with no depth limit and compare its training MAE with its test MAE.
2. Retrain it with `max_depth` values of 3, 5, 10 and 20 and plot training vs test MAE to see where overfitting starts.
3. Train a `RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=100, max_depth=12, random_state=42)` and compare it with Linear Regression and your best tree using `cross_val_score(..., scoring='neg_mean_absolute_error')`.
4. Add one new feature, such as the bedroom-to-room ratio (`AveBedrms / AveRooms`), and check whether it improves your best model.
5. Plot the feature importances of the random forest as a horizontal bar chart.
6. Evaluate only the final chosen model on the test set and save it with `joblib.dump(model, 'price_model.joblib')`.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The depth plot clearly shows the gap between training and test error growing for deep trees
- [ ] At least 3 models are compared with 5-fold cross-validation on the training data
- [ ] The best model has a lower test MAE than your Week 1 Linear Regression
- [ ] The README explains overfitting in your own words using your plot
- [ ] `price_model.joblib` loads in a fresh notebook and makes predictions

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- `cross_val_score` returns negative MAE, so multiply it by -1 before reporting it.
- A training MAE close to zero with a much larger test MAE is the classic sign of overfitting.
- Limiting `max_depth` keeps the saved random forest file small enough to push to GitHub.
- Pass `n_jobs=-1` to the random forest to use all your CPU cores.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Try `HistGradientBoostingRegressor` and see whether it beats your random forest.

### 📤 Submission
Run all cells so every output and chart is visible, then share your notebook: in Colab use **Share → Anyone with the link**, on Kaggle set it to **Public** (or save it to GitHub with a short README). Share a LinkedIn post with 2–3 key charts or results (or a 30–60 second demo once you have an app), put the notebook link in the post or its first comment, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Compared Linear Regression, decision trees and random forests with cross-validation
Diagnosed overfitting by plotting training vs test error across tree depths
Identified the features that drive house prices using feature importance

3.title: House Price Web App with Streamlit
deliverables: A Streamlit app that predicts a price from user inputs
A chart showing the prediction against the price distribution
Input validation and a clear message for a missing model file
A `requirements.txt` and a README with run instructions and screenshots
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same notebook or project.

You will build a Streamlit app where a user sets house features with sliders and instantly sees a predicted price. You will also make the app robust by validating input and handling missing files cleanly.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Building an interactive form with Streamlit widgets
- Matching app input to the exact feature order the model expects
- Validating input and setting sensible value ranges
- Handling errors such as a missing model file

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create `app.py` and load `price_model.joblib` in a function with `@st.cache_resource`, showing `st.error` if the file is missing.
2. Add sliders or number inputs for each feature, using the minimum and maximum from the training data as limits.
3. Build a one-row DataFrame from the inputs with the same column names and order as training (including your Week 2 feature), then call `predict`.
4. Display the prediction as a dollar amount with `st.metric`, clearly labelled as an estimate.
5. Add a histogram of all house prices with a vertical line showing where the prediction falls.
6. Add input checks, such as warning when bedrooms exceed rooms, and skip the prediction until the input makes sense.
7. Test 5 input combinations, including extreme values, and note any odd predictions in the README.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] `streamlit run app.py` starts the app with no errors after installing from `requirements.txt`
- [ ] Changing any input updates the predicted price
- [ ] The app's prediction for a test row matches the notebook's prediction for the same row
- [ ] Impossible input shows a warning instead of a prediction
- [ ] Deleting the model file shows a clear error message instead of a crash

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If predictions look wrong, print your input DataFrame and compare its columns with `model.feature_names_in_`.
- Multiply the prediction by 100,000 before showing it as a dollar amount.
- The [Streamlit docs](https://streamlit.io) cover `st.slider`, `st.metric` and caching with short examples.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'Compare two houses' mode that shows two predictions side by side.

### 📤 Submission
Run all cells so every output and chart is visible, then share your notebook: in Colab use **Share → Anyone with the link**, on Kaggle set it to **Public** (or save it to GitHub with a short README). Share a LinkedIn post with 2–3 key charts or results (or a 30–60 second demo once you have an app), put the notebook link in the post or its first comment, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a Streamlit web app that predicts house prices from interactive sliders
Connected a saved scikit-learn model to a user interface with matching feature handling
Added input validation and error handling so the app behaves sensibly on bad input

4.title: Capstone: What-If Explorer and Final Polish
deliverables: A what-if chart section in the app
A map of house locations
A final README with results and limitations
A 60-second demo video
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same notebook or project.

You will add a what-if explorer that shows how the predicted price changes as one feature changes, plus a map of the houses. You finish with a polished README and a demo video that walks through your project.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Using a model to answer 'what if' questions
- Plotting data on a map with latitude and longitude
- Explaining model behaviour in plain language
- Presenting a project with a README and demo

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write a function that takes the current inputs, varies one chosen feature across 30 values between its minimum and maximum, and returns the predicted price for each.
2. Test the function in a notebook first and plot the result as a line chart, such as price vs median income.
3. Add a 'What-if' section to the app with a dropdown to pick the feature and a line chart with the current value marked.
4. Add a map of a 2,000-house sample using `st.map` with the latitude and longitude columns.
5. Write a short 'What drives price?' section in the app that explains your feature importance and what-if findings in plain words.
6. Polish the layout with inputs in the sidebar, clear headings, and a note that estimates are based on 1990 census data.
7. Finish the README with a summary, screenshots, your Week 2 results table, how to run it and its limitations.
8. Record a 60-second demo: change sliders, use the what-if chart and show the map.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Choosing a feature in the what-if dropdown draws a line chart of predicted price across its range
- [ ] The map shows at least 1,000 houses without slowing the app noticeably
- [ ] The app explains in plain words which features matter most
- [ ] A new person can install and run the app by following the README
- [ ] The demo video is under 90 seconds and shows the app working live

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Build all 30 input rows as one DataFrame and call `predict` once, which is much faster than 30 separate calls.
- Tree models give step-shaped what-if lines; that is expected and worth explaining in your demo.
- `st.map` expects columns named `latitude` and `longitude` (or `lat` and `lon`), so rename them first.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Deploy the app for free on Streamlit Community Cloud and add the live link to your README.

### 📤 Submission
Run all cells so every output and chart is visible, then share your notebook: in Colab use **Share → Anyone with the link**, on Kaggle set it to **Public** (or save it to GitHub with a short README). Share a LinkedIn post with 2–3 key charts or results (or a 30–60 second demo once you have an app), put the notebook link in the post or its first comment, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a what-if explorer that shows how predicted house prices change with each feature
Added an interactive map of California housing data to my Streamlit app
Shipped a documented house price prediction app with a live demo

node.project_name: CloudVault: RESTful Secure API & Resource Management Hub
node.tagline: Build a REST API with Node.js and Express that stores your notes and links, and keeps each user's items private with a login.

1.title: Your First Express API
deliverables: A Node + Express project that starts with `node server.js` or `npm start`
Three working GET routes: list, single item, and filter by type
A `.gitignore` that excludes `node_modules`
A short demo video calling the routes in Thunder Client or Postman
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Set up a Node.js project with Express and build your first API endpoints that return vault items (notes and links) from an in-memory array. You will learn how a server receives a request and sends back JSON.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Setting up a Node project with `npm init` and installing packages
- Creating an Express server and defining routes
- Sending JSON responses and using route parameters like `/items/:id`
- Testing an API with a browser and Thunder Client or Postman

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a folder, run `npm init -y` and `npm install express`, and add `node_modules` to a `.gitignore` file.
2. Create `server.js` that starts an Express app on port 3000 and responds to `GET /` with `{ message: 'CloudVault API is running' }`.
3. Add an `items` array with 4-5 sample objects like `{ id, title, type, content }`, where `type` is `note` or `link`.
4. Add `GET /api/items` that returns all items as JSON.
5. Add `GET /api/items/:id` that returns one item, or a 404 status with `{ error: 'Item not found' }` if the id does not exist.
6. Add `GET /api/items?type=note` support by filtering on `req.query.type` inside the list route.
7. Test every route in the browser and in Thunder Client or Postman, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] `GET /api/items` returns all sample items as JSON
- [ ] `GET /api/items/1` returns one item and `GET /api/items/999` returns status 404 with an error message
- [ ] `GET /api/items?type=link` returns only links
- [ ] `node_modules` is not committed to Git
- [ ] The server logs a message showing which port it is running on

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- `req.params.id` is always a string, so convert it with `Number()` before comparing with numeric ids.
- Install `nodemon` as a dev dependency and add a `dev` script so the server restarts when you save.
- Thunder Client is a free VS Code extension that is quicker to set up than Postman.
- The 'Getting started' guide on [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com) covers routing basics.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `GET /api/stats` route that returns how many notes and how many links exist.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built my first REST API with Node.js and Express
Created routes with URL parameters, query filters and proper 404 responses
Tested API endpoints using Thunder Client

2.title: Full CRUD, Validation & Middleware
deliverables: Working create, read, update and delete routes for items
Validation with clear 400 error messages
A custom logger middleware
An exported Thunder Client or Postman collection in the repo
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Turn your read-only API into a full CRUD API so items can be created, updated and deleted, with input validation and correct status codes. You will also write your first custom middleware.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- The four CRUD operations mapped to POST, GET, PUT/PATCH and DELETE
- Reading JSON request bodies with `express.json()`
- Validating input and returning the right HTTP status codes (200, 201, 400, 404)
- What middleware is and how to write a simple logger

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add `app.use(express.json())` near the top of `server.js` so `req.body` works.
2. Add `POST /api/items` that creates an item with a new id and returns it with status 201.
3. Validate the body: `title` is required and under 100 characters, `type` must be `note` or `link`, and links must have a `content` starting with `http`; return 400 with a clear message otherwise.
4. Add `PUT /api/items/:id` to update an item (with the same validation) and `DELETE /api/items/:id` to remove it, returning 404 for unknown ids.
5. Write a logger middleware that prints the method, URL and time of every request, and register it with `app.use`.
6. Move the item routes into `routes/items.js` using `express.Router()` to keep `server.js` short.
7. Test every route, including bad input, and save your requests as a Thunder Client or Postman collection.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Creating an item returns status 201 and the new item
- [ ] Posting an item without a title returns status 400 and a helpful error
- [ ] Updating or deleting an unknown id returns status 404
- [ ] Every request is printed in the terminal by your logger
- [ ] Item routes live in their own router file

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If `req.body` is `undefined`, you forgot `express.json()` or did not set the `Content-Type: application/json` header.
- Write a small `validateItem(body)` function that returns an error message or `null`, and reuse it for POST and PUT.
- Always call `next()` at the end of your middleware or requests will hang.
- Read the 'Using middleware' guide on [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `tags` array to items and support `GET /api/items?tag=study`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a full CRUD REST API with Node.js and Express
Added input validation and correct HTTP status codes for every route
Wrote custom logging middleware and organised routes with Express Router

3.title: Saving Data with SQLite & Error Handling
deliverables: A SQLite-backed API where data survives restarts
Search and pagination on the list route
A central error-handling middleware
A demo video creating an item, restarting the server and fetching it again
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace the in-memory array with a SQLite database so your data survives a server restart. You will also add search, simple pagination and a central error handler so the API behaves well when things go wrong.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Storing data in a SQLite database with basic SQL (CREATE, INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE)
- Using parameterised queries to avoid SQL injection
- Pagination and search with query parameters
- Central error-handling middleware in Express

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install `better-sqlite3` and create `db.js` that opens `vault.db` and runs `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS items (...)`.
2. Rewrite each route to use SQL with `?` placeholders, for example `db.prepare('SELECT * FROM items WHERE id = ?').get(id)`.
3. Restart the server and confirm items you created are still there.
4. Add `GET /api/items?search=react` using `WHERE title LIKE ?` with `%` around the search term.
5. Add pagination with `?page=1&limit=10` using `LIMIT` and `OFFSET`, and return `{ page, limit, total, items }`.
6. Add an error-handling middleware `(err, req, res, next)` at the end of `server.js` that logs the error and returns status 500 with a generic message.
7. Test search, pagination, restarts and a deliberately broken query to see the error handler work.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Items created before a server restart are still returned after it
- [ ] All SQL queries use placeholders instead of string concatenation
- [ ] `?search=` returns only matching items and `?page=2&limit=5` returns the correct slice
- [ ] Any unexpected error returns status 500 with JSON instead of crashing the server
- [ ] The `.db` file is listed in `.gitignore`

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If `better-sqlite3` fails to install on your machine, store the data in a `data.json` file with `fs/promises` instead and keep the same routes.
- Use a free tool like DB Browser for SQLite to look inside your database file.
- Validate `page` and `limit` as positive numbers and cap `limit` at something like 50.
- SQL syntax is documented on [sqlite.org](https://sqlite.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `created_at` column and support `?sort=newest` and `?sort=oldest`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Connected my Express API to a SQLite database so data persists across restarts
Added search and pagination using safe parameterised SQL queries
Built central error-handling middleware to keep the API stable

4.title: User Login with JWT & API Docs
deliverables: Register and login routes with hashed passwords
An auth middleware protecting all item routes
Per-user items that other users cannot read or change
A README with setup steps and full endpoint documentation
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add user accounts so each person can register, log in and see only their own vault items. Finish by writing clear API documentation in your README and recording a full demo.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Hashing passwords with `bcryptjs` instead of storing them in plain text
- Issuing and checking JSON Web Tokens (JWT) with `jsonwebtoken`
- Protecting routes with an auth middleware
- Keeping secrets in environment variables with a `.env` file

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install `bcryptjs`, `jsonwebtoken` and `dotenv`, and put a `JWT_SECRET` in a `.env` file that is listed in `.gitignore`.
2. Create a `users` table and a `POST /api/auth/register` route that validates email and password length and stores a bcrypt hash.
3. Create `POST /api/auth/login` that checks the password with `bcrypt.compare` and returns a token signed with `jwt.sign`.
4. Write an `auth` middleware that reads the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, verifies it, and sets `req.user` or returns 401.
5. Add a `user_id` column to items, protect all item routes with the middleware, and make every query filter by `req.user.id`.
6. Write a README with setup steps, a `.env.example`, and a table of every endpoint with an example request and response.
7. Record a demo: register, log in, create items, and show that a second user cannot see the first user's items.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Passwords are stored only as bcrypt hashes
- [ ] Calling an item route without a valid token returns status 401
- [ ] User A cannot read, update or delete User B's items
- [ ] The `.env` file is not committed, and a `.env.example` is
- [ ] Someone else could run the project by following the README alone

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use `bcryptjs` rather than `bcrypt` because it is pure JavaScript and installs easily on Windows.
- Give tokens an expiry like `{ expiresIn: '1h' }` and return the same vague error for a wrong email or password.
- Load `dotenv` at the very top of `server.js` with `require('dotenv').config()`.
- Node.js docs are at [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/docs) and Express guides at [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a simple rate limit on the login route with the `express-rate-limit` package.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added secure user registration and login with bcrypt and JWT to my Node.js API
Protected routes with auth middleware so each user only sees their own data
Documented every endpoint with example requests in a clear README

node.project_name: ChatPulse: Real-Time WebSockets Messaging & Collab Server
node.tagline: Build a real-time chat app with Node.js, Express and Socket.IO, with chat rooms, saved history and a simple web page to chat from.

1.title: A Simple Message Board with Express
deliverables: An Express server that serves a chat page from `public/`
GET and POST message routes
A web page that shows and sends messages
A demo video posting messages from two tabs
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Build an Express server that stores messages in memory and serves a basic web page where people can post and read messages. This gives you a working chat without real-time features, so you understand the request-response model before moving to WebSockets.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Setting up a Node project and an Express server
- Serving static HTML, CSS and JavaScript files with `express.static`
- Building GET and POST API routes with in-memory data
- Calling your own API from the browser with `fetch`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Run `npm init -y` and `npm install express`, add a `.gitignore` for `node_modules`, and create `server.js`.
2. Create a `public/` folder with `index.html`, `style.css` and `app.js`, and serve it with `app.use(express.static('public'))`.
3. Add a `messages` array and a `GET /api/messages` route that returns it.
4. Add `POST /api/messages` that accepts `{ name, text }`, adds a timestamp, pushes it to the array and returns status 201.
5. In `index.html`, build a message list, a name input, a text input and a Send button.
6. In `app.js`, load messages with `fetch` on page load, send new messages with a POST, and reload the list after sending.
7. Open the page in two browser tabs, send messages from both, and notice you must refresh to see the other tab's messages.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Opening `http://localhost:3000` shows the chat page
- [ ] `GET /api/messages` returns all messages as JSON
- [ ] Sending a message adds it with a name, text and timestamp
- [ ] Empty messages are rejected with status 400
- [ ] `node_modules` is not committed

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Add `app.use(express.json())` or `req.body` will be `undefined` in your POST route.
- Display timestamps with `new Date(msg.time).toLocaleTimeString()`.
- Use `textContent` instead of `innerHTML` when showing messages so users cannot inject HTML.
- See 'Serving static files' on [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Make the page fetch new messages automatically every 3 seconds with `setInterval` and notice the downsides of polling.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a message board app with Node.js and Express
Served a front-end page and connected it to my own REST API with fetch
Learned the request-response model before moving to real-time chat

2.title: Going Real-Time with Socket.IO
deliverables: A Socket.IO server and client
Instant message delivery to all open tabs
Nicknames and join/leave notices
A demo video with two windows side by side chatting in real time
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace the refresh-to-see-messages approach with Socket.IO so messages appear instantly in every open browser. You will learn how real-time events work and how the server broadcasts to all connected users.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- What WebSockets are and how they differ from normal HTTP requests
- Setting up Socket.IO on the server and in the browser
- Emitting and listening for custom events
- Broadcasting to all clients or to everyone except the sender

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install `socket.io`, create an HTTP server with `http.createServer(app)`, and attach Socket.IO to it.
2. Load the client with `<script src="/socket.io/socket.io.js"></script>` and call `io()` in `app.js`.
3. Log a message on the server when a user connects and disconnects to confirm it works.
4. Ask for a nickname when the page opens and send it to the server with a `join` event.
5. On send, emit a `chat message` event; on the server, add it to the array and use `io.emit` to send it to everyone.
6. Broadcast 'Asha joined' and 'Asha left' notices using `socket.broadcast.emit` on join and disconnect.
7. Test with 2-3 tabs and confirm messages appear everywhere instantly without refreshing.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] A message sent in one tab appears in all other tabs within a second, without refreshing
- [ ] Each message shows the sender's nickname
- [ ] Join and leave notices appear for other users
- [ ] New users still see earlier messages when they join (sent from the in-memory array)
- [ ] The server does not crash when a tab is closed

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use `server.listen(3000)` instead of `app.listen` once Socket.IO is attached, or the client script will not load.
- Store the nickname on the socket (`socket.data.name = name`) so you know who left on `disconnect`.
- Send existing messages to only the new user with `socket.emit('history', messages)`.
- The official guide and chat tutorial are on [socket.io](https://socket.io).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Show your own messages on the right and others' on the left, like a messaging app.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Upgraded my Node.js chat app to real-time messaging with Socket.IO
Broadcast messages and join/leave notices to all connected users instantly
Learned how WebSockets differ from regular HTTP requests

3.title: Chat Rooms & Saved Message History
deliverables: Three working chat rooms
Message history stored in SQLite and loaded per room
Server-side validation with error feedback to the sender
A demo video switching rooms and restarting the server to show saved history
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add chat rooms so users can join different channels, and save messages to a SQLite database so history survives a server restart. You will also validate incoming events so bad data cannot break the server.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Socket.IO rooms with `socket.join` and `io.to(room).emit`
- Saving and loading data with SQLite and parameterised queries
- Validating data that arrives through socket events
- Handling errors so one bad event does not crash the server

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add a room picker on the page with 3 fixed rooms such as General, Study and Random.
2. When a user picks a room, call `socket.join(room)` on the server and leave the previous room.
3. Send chat messages only to that room with `io.to(room).emit(...)`.
4. Install `better-sqlite3`, create a `messages` table (id, room, name, text, created_at), and insert every message using `?` placeholders.
5. When a user joins a room, load the last 50 messages for that room from the database and send them only to that user.
6. Validate every message on the server (text not empty, under 500 characters, room is one of the allowed rooms), and emit an `error message` event back to the sender if invalid.
7. Wrap database calls in `try`/`catch`, restart the server, and confirm history is still there.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Messages in one room do not appear in other rooms
- [ ] Switching rooms shows that room's recent history
- [ ] History is still there after restarting the server
- [ ] Sending an empty or very long message shows an error to the sender only
- [ ] All SQL uses placeholders and the `.db` file is in `.gitignore`

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If `better-sqlite3` will not install, save messages to a `messages.json` file with `fs/promises` instead.
- Store the current room on `socket.data.room` so you know which room to leave when switching.
- Never trust data from the browser, even from your own page, because anyone can send socket events.
- See the Rooms section of the docs on [socket.io](https://socket.io).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Let users create a new room by typing a name, with validation on allowed characters.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added chat rooms to my real-time app using Socket.IO rooms

4.title: Typing Indicators, Online Users & Docs
deliverables: A live online-users list per room
A typing indicator that appears and disappears correctly
A polished, mobile-friendly chat page
A README documenting setup and all socket events
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add the features that make chat feel alive: a live list of online users in each room and a 'someone is typing' indicator. Then polish the UI and write a README that documents your socket events so others can run and extend your server.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Tracking connected users on the server with a `Map`
- Throttling frequent events like typing with timers
- Keeping server state correct when users disconnect
- Documenting a real-time API (event names and payloads)

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Keep a `Map` of socket id to `{ name, room }` and update it on join, room switch and disconnect.
2. After every change, emit a `room users` event with the list of names in that room and show it in a sidebar.
3. In the browser, emit `typing` when the user types, and `stop typing` after 1-2 seconds without a keypress using `setTimeout`.
4. On the server, forward typing events to others in the room, and show 'Asha is typing...' under the message list.
5. Polish the UI: auto-scroll to the newest message, disable Send for empty input, and make the page usable on a phone.
6. Write a README with setup steps, screenshots, and a table of every socket event, who sends it and what data it carries.
7. Record a final demo with two or three windows showing rooms, history, online users and typing indicators.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The online list updates within a second when someone joins, switches room or closes their tab
- [ ] The typing indicator shows for other users only and disappears after the user stops typing
- [ ] The chat auto-scrolls to new messages
- [ ] The README lists every socket event with its payload
- [ ] Someone else can run the project by following the README alone

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Clear the previous timer with `clearTimeout` on every keypress so `stop typing` fires only after a real pause.
- Remove the user from your `Map` in the `disconnect` handler or ghost users will stay online.
- Use `socket.to(room).emit` for typing so the sender does not see their own indicator.
- The Socket.IO docs on [socket.io](https://socket.io) have an emit cheatsheet that helps with broadcasting.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add emoji reactions to messages that update live for everyone in the room.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built ChatPulse, a real-time chat server with rooms and saved history using Node.js and Socket.IO
Added live online-user lists and typing indicators
Documented every socket event so others can run and extend the project

deliverables: An Express server with create, list and redirect routes

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Set up an Express server that can create short codes for long URLs and redirect visitors, using an in-memory array. You will learn how routes, request bodies and redirects work in a real, useful app.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Setting up a Node project and an Express server
- Reading JSON request bodies with `express.json()`
- Route parameters and HTTP redirects with `res.redirect`
- Generating random short codes in JavaScript

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Run `npm init -y` and `npm install express`, add a `.gitignore`, and create `server.js` listening on port 3000.
2. Create a `links` array to hold objects like `{ code, url, createdAt }`.
3. Write a `makeCode()` function that returns a random 6-character string of letters and numbers.
4. Add `POST /api/links` that reads `url` from the body, creates a link with a new code, and returns it with status 201.
5. Add `GET /api/links` that returns all links as JSON.
6. Add `GET /:code` that finds the link and calls `res.redirect(link.url)`, or returns 404 if the code is unknown.
7. Create a link with Thunder Client or Postman, then open `http://localhost:3000/<code>` in your browser to see the redirect.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] `POST /api/links` returns status 201 with the new code
- [ ] Opening `/<code>` in a browser redirects to the original URL
- [ ] An unknown code returns status 404 with a message
- [ ] `GET /api/links` lists every created link

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Build codes by picking random characters from a string like `'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789'` with `Math.random()`.
- Define `GET /:code` after your `/api` routes so it does not catch API requests by mistake.
- Use `nodemon` during development so the server restarts on save.
- Routing and `res.redirect` are explained on [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Make sure a newly generated code never matches an existing one.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a URL shortener API with Node.js and Express
Implemented short-code generation and HTTP redirects
Tested API routes with Thunder Client and live browser redirects

2.title: Full CRUD, Custom Aliases & Validation
deliverables: Create, read, update and delete routes for links
Custom alias support with duplicate checks
URL validation with clear error messages
An exported API collection in the repo
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Complete the API so links can be viewed, edited and deleted, and let users choose their own custom alias. You will add proper validation and status codes so the API gives helpful errors instead of silently accepting bad data.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Mapping CRUD actions to GET, POST, PUT and DELETE
- Validating URLs with the built-in `URL` class
- Using status codes 400, 404 and 409 correctly
- Writing and registering custom middleware

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Validate the `url` in `POST /api/links` by trying `new URL(url)` inside `try`/`catch`, and only allow `http:` and `https:` protocols.
2. Accept an optional `alias`; allow only letters, numbers and hyphens (3-20 characters), and return 409 if it is already taken.
3. Add `GET /api/links/:code` to return one link's details.
4. Add `PUT /api/links/:code` to change the target URL (with the same validation) and `DELETE /api/links/:code` to remove a link.
5. Write a logger middleware that prints the method, path and response time of each request.
6. Move the API routes into `routes/links.js` using `express.Router()`.
7. Test every success and error case and save them as a Thunder Client or Postman collection.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Creating a link with an invalid URL returns status 400 and a helpful message
- [ ] Creating a link with a taken alias returns status 409
- [ ] Updating a link changes where its short code redirects
- [ ] Deleting a link makes its short code return 404
- [ ] Every request is logged by your middleware

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- `new URL('hello')` throws an error, which makes it an easy validity check.
- A regular expression like `/^[a-zA-Z0-9-]{3,20}$/` checks alias rules in one line.
- Reserve words like `api` so nobody can create an alias that clashes with your routes.
- See the `URL` reference on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org) and middleware guides on [expressjs.com](https://expressjs.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add an optional `expiresAt` date after which the link returns 410 Gone.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Completed a full CRUD API for my URL shortener with Express Router
Added custom aliases with validation and duplicate detection
Used proper HTTP status codes and custom logging middleware

3.title: Saving Links in SQLite & Click Tracking
deliverables: A SQLite-backed link store
Click counting on every redirect
A stats route and a popular-links sort
A demo video clicking a link several times and showing the stats
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Store links in a SQLite database so they survive restarts, and count every click so users can see how popular each link is. You will also add a central error handler so the API fails gracefully.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Creating tables and running queries with SQLite
- Parameterised queries to prevent SQL injection
- Updating a counter on every request
- Central error-handling middleware in Express

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install `better-sqlite3` and create `db.js` that creates a `links` table with `code` (unique), `url`, `clicks` (default 0) and `created_at` columns.
2. Rewrite each route to use SQL with `?` placeholders instead of the array.
3. In the redirect route, run `UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1, last_clicked = ? WHERE code = ?` before redirecting.
4. Add `GET /api/links/:code/stats` that returns the clicks, creation date and last click time.
5. Add `GET /api/links?sort=popular` that orders links by clicks, highest first.
6. Add an error-handling middleware at the end of `server.js` that logs errors and returns status 500 as JSON.
7. Restart the server to confirm links and click counts are kept, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Links still work after a server restart
- [ ] Each visit to a short link increases its click count by 1
- [ ] The stats route returns clicks and dates for a link
- [ ] `?sort=popular` returns links ordered by clicks
- [ ] Unexpected errors return JSON with status 500 instead of crashing the server

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- The `UNIQUE` constraint on `code` gives you duplicate protection at the database level too.
- If `better-sqlite3` will not install, keep the links in a `links.json` file with `fs/promises` instead.
- Browsers may request `/favicon.ico`, which hits your `/:code` route, so ignore that path.
- SQL syntax is documented on [sqlite.org](https://sqlite.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Store each click in a separate `clicks` table and return clicks per day for the last 7 days.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Moved my URL shortener to a SQLite database for persistent storage
Added click tracking and a stats endpoint for every short link
Built central error handling to keep the API stable

4.title: Web Dashboard, API Key & Docs
deliverables: A web page for shortening links and viewing stats
A Copy-to-clipboard button for new short links
API-key protection on edit and delete routes
A README with setup steps and endpoint documentation
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Build a simple web page served by your Express app where anyone can shorten a link and see its stats, and protect edit and delete routes with an API key. Finish with a README that documents every endpoint.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Serving a front-end from Express with `express.static`
- Calling your API from the browser with `fetch`
- Protecting routes with a simple API-key middleware
- Keeping secrets in a `.env` file and writing API documentation

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create `public/index.html` with a form (URL and optional alias) and serve it with `express.static`.
2. In `public/app.js`, submit the form with `fetch`, show the new short link with a Copy button using `navigator.clipboard.writeText`, and show any error message from the API.
3. Add a table below the form that lists links with their click counts, loaded from `GET /api/links`.
4. Install `dotenv`, put an `ADMIN_KEY` in `.env`, and write a middleware that checks the `x-api-key` header.
5. Apply the API-key middleware only to the PUT and DELETE routes, returning 401 when the key is missing or wrong.
6. Write a README with setup steps, a `.env.example`, screenshots, and a table of every endpoint with an example request and response.
7. Record a final demo: shorten a link on the web page, open it, and show the click count going up.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Links can be created from the web page without Thunder Client or Postman
- [ ] API errors such as a bad URL are shown on the page
- [ ] PUT and DELETE return 401 without the correct `x-api-key` header
- [ ] The `.env` file is not committed, and a `.env.example` is
- [ ] Someone else can run the project by following the README alone

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Register `express.static` before your `/:code` route so `index.html` and `app.js` load correctly.
- Refresh the links table after creating a link so the new one appears straight away.
- Load `dotenv` at the very top of `server.js` with `require('dotenv').config()`.
- Node.js documentation lives at [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/docs).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Generate a QR code for each short link using the free `qrcode` npm package and show it on the page.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built LinkShort, a full URL shortener with Node.js, Express and SQLite
Created a web dashboard for shortening links and tracking clicks
Protected admin routes with API-key middleware and documented every endpoint

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Write a small Python program that reads a CSV file of expenses and prints useful totals in the terminal. This is the foundation of the whole project, and it practises the everyday Python skills (functions, loops, files and dictionaries) that every later week depends on.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Reading files safely with `with open(...)` and the built-in `csv` module
- Splitting a program into small functions that each do one job
- Using dictionaries to group and total values by category
- Building a simple text menu with `input()` and a `while` loop

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a project folder with `main.py` and a `data/expenses.csv` file containing 15-20 sample rows with the columns `date,category,description,amount`.
2. Write a `load_expenses(path)` function that uses `csv.DictReader` to return a list of dictionaries, and print the result to check it works.
3. Convert the `amount` column to `float` inside the loader so every later calculation gets numbers, not strings.
4. Write `total_spent(expenses)` and `totals_by_category(expenses)` functions, and test each one by printing its result before moving on.
5. Add a `biggest_expense(expenses)` function that returns the single largest row.
6. Build a menu loop in `main()` with options like `1) Show all  2) Totals by category  3) Biggest expense  4) Quit`.
7. Print results in neat aligned columns using f-strings such as `f'{category:<12} {amount:>8.2f}'`.
8. Commit your code to a Git repo with a short README explaining how to run `python main.py`.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Running `python main.py` shows a menu and each option prints the correct result
- [ ] The category totals add up to the overall total printed by the program
- [ ] Choosing Quit exits cleanly without an error
- [ ] The code has at least four functions and no copy-pasted logic

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If your totals look like text glued together, you forgot to convert `amount` to `float`.
- Use `totals[cat] = totals.get(cat, 0) + amount` to add to a category without a `KeyError`.
- The [Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/) have a short, readable page on the `csv` module; search for `csv.DictReader`.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a menu option that shows totals per month by taking the first 7 characters of the date (for example `2025-03`).

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a menu-driven Python CLI that reads expense data from a CSV file
Wrote reusable functions to calculate totals, category breakdowns and the biggest expense
Formatted clean terminal reports using f-strings and dictionaries

deliverables: `tracker.py`, `storage.py` and `main.py` modules with classes in use

2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Reorganise your code into classes and modules, and make it handle messy real-world data. You will also let users add new expenses and export a report, so the tool starts to feel like a real app.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Writing classes with `__init__` and methods (an `Expense` and an `ExpenseTracker`)
- Splitting code into modules and importing between files
- Cleaning and validating data such as blank rows, bad numbers and extra spaces
- Writing data back to files as CSV and JSON

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create an `Expense` class with `date`, `category`, `description` and `amount` attributes, plus a `__str__` method for nice printing.
2. Create an `ExpenseTracker` class that holds a list of `Expense` objects, and move your Week 1 functions into it as methods.
3. Move the classes into `tracker.py` and file reading and writing into `storage.py`, keeping only the menu in `main.py`.
4. Add a few messy rows to your CSV (an empty amount, `abc` as an amount, ` Food ` with spaces) and update the loader to skip or fix them while counting how many rows were skipped.
5. Add an `Add expense` menu option that asks for each field, validates the amount, and appends the new row to the CSV.
6. Add a `Search` option that finds expenses whose description contains a keyword, ignoring upper and lower case.
7. Add an `Export report` option that writes the category totals to `report.json` using the `json` module.
8. Re-run every menu option after the refactor to make sure nothing from Week 1 broke.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The program runs without crashing on a CSV that contains blank and invalid rows
- [ ] A newly added expense still appears after you quit and restart the program
- [ ] Searching for a word finds matches regardless of capital letters
- [ ] `report.json` opens and contains the correct category totals
- [ ] `main.py` contains only menu code and the logic lives in the classes

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Wrap `float(value)` in `try/except ValueError` to catch bad numbers without crashing.
- Use `.strip().title()` to normalise categories so ` food ` and `Food` count as the same category.
- If `import tracker` fails, make sure you are running Python from inside the project folder.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Let the user set a monthly budget per category and show a warning next to any category that goes over it.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Refactored my Python expense tool into classes and separate modules
Added data cleaning that safely skips invalid rows instead of crashing
Built add, search and JSON export features into the command-line app

3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace the CSV file with a real SQLite database using Python's built-in `sqlite3` module, and add proper command-line arguments. This teaches you how most apps store data and how to make a program fail gracefully.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Creating tables and running `INSERT` and `SELECT` queries with `sqlite3`
- Using parameterised queries (`?` placeholders) to avoid SQL injection
- Handling errors with `try/except` and giving clear messages
- Adding command-line arguments and subcommands with `argparse`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a `db.py` module with a function that connects to `expenses.db` and creates an `expenses` table if it does not exist.
2. Write `add_expense`, `get_all` and `totals_by_category` functions using SQL, with `GROUP BY category` for the totals.
3. Write an `import_csv(path)` function that loads your old CSV into the database, reusing your Week 2 cleaning logic.
4. Update `ExpenseTracker` to read from and write to the database instead of the CSV file.
5. Add `argparse` subcommands so users can run `python main.py import data/expenses.csv`, `python main.py summary` and `python main.py add`.
6. Handle likely failures (missing file, wrong columns, bad amount) with `try/except` and a friendly one-line message instead of a traceback.
7. Add a `--month 2025-03` filter to `summary` using a `WHERE date LIKE ?` query.
8. Test each command in the terminal, including at least two deliberate mistakes such as a wrong file path.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Running `import` twice on the same file does not crash and either skips duplicates or shows a clear message
- [ ] `summary` prints the same totals as your Week 2 version for the same data
- [ ] Passing a file that does not exist prints a clear error, not a Python traceback
- [ ] All SQL uses `?` placeholders instead of f-strings
- [ ] `python main.py --help` lists all the commands

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Call `conn.commit()` after an `INSERT`, or your new rows will disappear when the program ends.
- The free DB Browser for SQLite app lets you look inside `expenses.db` to check your data.
- Read the `sqlite3` and `argparse` pages in the [Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/); both include short examples.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `delete <id>` command and an `export --format csv` command that writes the database back out to a CSV file.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Moved my Python expense tracker from CSV files to a SQLite database
Built a command-line interface with argparse subcommands and filters
Added error handling so the tool shows clear messages instead of crashing

This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Put a small web dashboard on top of your database using Flask, and protect your core logic with a few automated tests. You finish with a complete, documented project that you can demo in under a minute.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

1.title: System Health Snapshot
deliverables: `monitor.py` with at least four functions
A printed health report in the terminal
`health_log.txt` showing several runs
A README with how to run it and a sample output
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Write a Python script that prints a quick health report of your computer (disk space, folder sizes and the largest files) and saves a summary to a log file. You will practise core Python using only the standard library, so there is nothing to install.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Using the `os`, `shutil` and `datetime` standard-library modules
- Walking through folders with `os.walk` and working with file sizes
- Writing reusable functions with parameters and return values
- Appending lines to a log file

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create `monitor.py` and write a `disk_usage(path)` function using `shutil.disk_usage` that returns total, used and free space in GB.
2. Write a `folder_size(path)` function that uses `os.walk` to add up the size of every file in a folder, and test it on your Downloads folder.
3. Write `largest_files(path, n)` that returns the `n` biggest files as a list of `(size, filepath)` tuples, largest first.
4. Write a helper `human_size(num_bytes)` that turns numbers like `5242880` into `5.0 MB`.
5. Print a neat report that combines all three checks with a timestamp from `datetime.now()`.
6. Append a one-line summary (time, free disk %, folder size) to `health_log.txt` every time the script runs.
7. Ask the user which folder to scan with `input()`, and fall back to the current folder if they just press Enter.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Running `python monitor.py` prints disk space, folder size and the top 5 largest files
- [ ] Sizes are shown in readable units (KB, MB, GB), not raw bytes
- [ ] Each run adds exactly one new line to `health_log.txt` without deleting old lines
- [ ] Entering a folder that does not exist prints a friendly message instead of crashing

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use `os.path.getsize(os.path.join(root, name))` inside the `os.walk` loop to get each file's size.
- Open the log with mode `'a'` (append), not `'w'`, or you will wipe out old entries.
- Some system files raise `PermissionError`, so wrap the size call in `try/except` and skip them.
- The `os` and `shutil` pages in the [Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/) have short examples.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a check that counts files by extension (for example 40 `.jpg` and 12 `.pdf`) in the scanned folder.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a Python system health script using only the standard library
Scanned folders with os.walk to report disk usage and the largest files
Logged timestamped health snapshots to a file on every run

2.title: Configurable Checks with Classes
deliverables: `checks.py` with a base class and at least three check subclasses
`config.json` that controls thresholds and folders
Colour-coded status output in the terminal
`history.json` with saved results from several runs
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Turn your script into a small monitoring tool where each check is a class that returns a clear OK, WARN or FAIL result. Settings move into a JSON config file, so users can change thresholds without touching the code.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Writing a simple base class and subclasses that share a method name
- Reading settings from a JSON config file
- Organising code into modules (`checks.py`, `config.py`, `main.py`)
- Using thresholds to turn raw numbers into a status

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a base class `Check` with a `name` and a `run()` method that returns a dictionary like `{'name': ..., 'status': 'OK', 'detail': ...}`.
2. Rewrite your Week 1 functions as subclasses (`DiskSpaceCheck`, `FolderSizeCheck`, `LargeFileCheck`), each with its own `run()`.
3. Create `config.json` with values like `min_free_percent`, `max_folder_mb` and the folders to watch, and load it in `config.py`.
4. Make each check return `WARN` or `FAIL` when a threshold is crossed, and `OK` otherwise.
5. In `main.py`, build a list of check objects from the config, loop over them, and print one coloured line per result using ANSI colour codes.
6. Save every run's results to `history.json` as a list, keeping only the last 50 runs.
7. Add a `--summary` option (or a menu choice) that reads `history.json` and prints how many times each check failed.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Changing a threshold in `config.json` changes the output without editing any Python code
- [ ] Every check returns the same dictionary shape (name, status, detail)
- [ ] Setting an impossible threshold makes that check show FAIL
- [ ] `history.json` never grows beyond 50 entries
- [ ] The summary option prints the correct failure counts

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If ANSI colours do not show on Windows, call `os.system('')` once at startup or use Windows Terminal.
- Use `json.dump(data, f, indent=2)` so your JSON files stay readable.
- Adding a new check should only mean writing a new class; if you have to edit the main loop, rethink the design.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `FileAgeCheck` that warns if a chosen backup folder has no files newer than 7 days.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Redesigned my Python monitor so each health check is its own class
Moved thresholds into a JSON config file so behaviour changes without code edits
Saved run history and built a failure summary report

3.title: Website Uptime Checks with requests
deliverables: A `WebsiteCheck` class integrated with the existing checks
A config with a list of sites to monitor
An `uptime.csv` log of website results
An uptime report showing percentage and average response time per site
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add website monitoring with the `requests` library: check whether sites respond, how fast they are, and what went wrong when they fail. Real networks are unreliable, so this week is all about handling errors properly.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Making HTTP GET requests with the `requests` library
- Understanding status codes (200, 404, 500) and response times
- Catching network errors like timeouts and connection failures
- Saving results to a CSV file for later analysis

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install requests (`pip install requests`), add it to `requirements.txt`, and try `requests.get('https://example.com', timeout=5)` in a small scratch script first.
2. Add a `sites` list to `config.json` with 5-8 URLs, including one made-up URL that will fail.
3. Create a `WebsiteCheck` class that sends a GET request, measures the response time, and returns OK for 2xx, WARN for slow responses and FAIL for errors or bad status codes.
4. Catch `requests.exceptions.Timeout`, `ConnectionError` and the general `RequestException` separately, and put a clear reason in the `detail` field.
5. Plug `WebsiteCheck` objects into your existing check loop so system and website checks print together.
6. Append each website result (time, URL, status code, response ms, status) to `uptime.csv` using the `csv` module.
7. Add a report option that reads `uptime.csv` and prints the uptime percentage and average response time for each site.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] A made-up or unreachable URL shows FAIL with a readable reason and the program keeps running
- [ ] Every request uses a timeout so the program never hangs
- [ ] The uptime percentages in the report match the rows in `uptime.csv`
- [ ] Turning off Wi-Fi and running the monitor produces FAIL results, not a crash

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Always pass `timeout=` to `requests.get`, because without it a request can wait forever.
- Use `response.elapsed.total_seconds()` or `time.perf_counter()` to measure the response time.
- `requests` does not raise an error for a 404 by default, so check `response.status_code` yourself.
- The [requests docs](https://requests.readthedocs.io) have a clear quickstart page.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Also check that each page contains an expected word (such as the site name) to catch pages that load but show an error.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added website uptime monitoring to my Python project using the requests library
Handled timeouts and connection errors so the monitor never crashes
Logged response times to CSV and generated per-site uptime reports

4.title: Scheduled Monitoring, Alerts and Tests
deliverables: A `watch` mode that runs checks on a schedule
Alert logic with `alerts.log` and recovery messages
An auto-generated `status.html` page
At least 4 passing pytest tests and a complete README
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Make PySentinel run on its own every minute or so, raise an alert when something stays broken, and publish a simple HTML status page. Add a few pytest tests and a good README so the project is ready to show.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Running tasks on a timer with a loop and `time.sleep`
- Simple alert logic that only fires after repeated failures
- Generating an HTML file from Python
- Writing unit tests with `pytest`, including faking a network call

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add a `watch` mode (`python main.py watch --every 60`) that runs all checks in a loop, sleeps between rounds, and stops cleanly on Ctrl+C.
2. Track consecutive failures per check and raise an alert only after 2 failures in a row, then print a `RECOVERED` message when it is OK again.
3. Write alerts to the terminal and to `alerts.log`.
4. After each round, write `status.html` with a table of every check, its status colour and the last-checked time, and open it in your browser.
5. Install pytest and write at least 4 tests: threshold logic, the alert counter, the uptime report maths, and a `WebsiteCheck` failure using `unittest.mock.patch` to fake `requests.get`.
6. Update the README with features, config options, screenshots of the terminal and status page, and how to run the tests.
7. Record a 30-60 second demo: start watch mode, add a broken site to the config, and show the alert and the status page updating.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Watch mode runs at least 3 rounds and exits cleanly with Ctrl+C
- [ ] A site that fails once does not alert, but a site that fails twice in a row does
- [ ] `status.html` opens in a browser and shows the latest results
- [ ] `pytest` passes with at least 4 tests, including one that fakes a network call
- [ ] No test makes a real internet request

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Catch `KeyboardInterrupt` around your loop to print a goodbye message instead of a traceback.
- Keep the alert counters in a dictionary like `{check_name: fail_count}`.
- Add `<meta http-equiv='refresh' content='60'>` to the HTML head so the status page reloads itself.
- The [pytest docs](https://docs.pytest.org) and the `unittest.mock` page in the [Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/) explain patching.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Serve the status page from a tiny Flask app instead of a static file, or show a desktop notification when an alert fires.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Turned my Python monitor into a scheduled watcher with failure alerts
Generated an auto-refreshing HTML status page for system and website checks
Wrote pytest tests with mocked network calls to verify my alert logic

python.tagline: Build a quiz and flashcard app that helps you revise any subject, starting in the terminal and ending as a small web app.

1.title: Terminal Quiz from a Text File
deliverables: `quiz.py` with separate functions for loading, asking and scoring
`questions.txt` with at least 10 questions
An end-of-quiz summary with score, percentage and wrong answers
A README explaining how to run the quiz and add questions
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Build a quiz game that reads questions from a file, asks them one by one, and shows your score at the end. It is small, fun to demo, and practises loops, conditions, functions and file reading.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Reading and parsing a text file line by line
- Using lists and dictionaries to store questions and answers
- Writing functions and `for`/`while` loops for game flow
- Comparing user input fairly by ignoring case and extra spaces

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create `questions.txt` with at least 10 questions in the format `question|answer`, one per line, on a subject you are studying.
2. Write `load_questions(path)` that reads the file, splits each line on `|`, and returns a list of dictionaries.
3. Write `ask_question(q)` that prints the question, reads the answer, and returns `True` or `False`.
4. Compare answers using `.strip().lower()` on both sides so `Paris`, ` paris ` and `PARIS` all count as correct.
5. Shuffle the questions with `random.shuffle` and let the user choose how many to answer.
6. Show the score and percentage at the end, plus a list of the questions they got wrong with the correct answers.
7. Add a `Play again? (y/n)` loop.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The quiz runs from start to finish and shows the correct score
- [ ] Answers are accepted regardless of capital letters or extra spaces
- [ ] Questions appear in a different order on each run
- [ ] Blank or badly formatted lines in `questions.txt` are skipped without crashing

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Call `line.strip()` before splitting so the newline character does not end up in the answer.
- If a line has no `|`, skip it and print a warning instead of crashing.
- The `random` page in the [Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/) explains `shuffle` and `sample`.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Support several accepted answers separated by commas, like `question|colour,color`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a terminal quiz game in Python that loads questions from a file
Added shuffling, scoring and a review of wrong answers
Practised functions, loops and string handling by building a revision tool

2.title: Decks, Classes and Saved Progress
deliverables: `models.py`, `storage.py` and `main.py` modules
`decks.json` with at least 2 decks and some multiple-choice questions
`progress.json` that stores results per player
A stats screen showing attempts and best score per deck
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Organise questions into decks (like DSA, DBMS or Python) using classes, and add multiple-choice questions. Save each player's progress to a JSON file so the app remembers how they did last time.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Designing classes (`Question`, `Deck`, `QuizSession`)
- Reading and writing JSON with the `json` module
- Splitting code into modules
- Tracking stats over time, such as attempts and best score

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Convert your questions into a `decks.json` file with at least 2 decks, where each question has `text`, `answer` and an optional `choices` list for multiple choice.
2. Create a `Question` class with a `check(answer)` method, and a `Deck` class that builds its questions from the JSON data.
3. For multiple-choice questions, print the options as `A) B) C) D)` and accept the letter as the answer.
4. Create a `QuizSession` class that runs one round and returns a result (deck, score, total, date).
5. Ask for the player's name at the start and save each result to `progress.json` under that name.
6. Add a main menu: choose deck, play, view my stats (attempts and best score per deck), quit.
7. Move the classes into `models.py` and file handling into `storage.py`, keeping the menu in `main.py`.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Players can pick a deck and answer both typed and multiple-choice questions
- [ ] Stats are still there after closing and reopening the program
- [ ] Two different player names keep separate stats
- [ ] A missing `progress.json` is created automatically on the first run

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Catch `FileNotFoundError` when loading `progress.json` and start with an empty dictionary.
- Store dates as strings with `datetime.now().isoformat()` because JSON cannot store datetime objects.
- Keep `print` and `input()` out of `Question` and `Deck` where possible so they are easy to test later.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'practise mistakes' mode that only asks the questions the player got wrong last time.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Refactored my Python quiz app into classes and separate modules
Added decks, multiple-choice questions and per-player progress saved as JSON
Built a stats screen that tracks attempts and best scores

3.title: Import Questions from a Free API
deliverables: `api.py` with a function that fetches and converts API questions
An `Online quiz` menu option with a difficulty choice
A fallback to local decks when the API is unavailable
The ability to save fetched questions as a local deck
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Connect QuizCraft to the free Open Trivia Database API so players can pull fresh questions on many topics. You will learn how to call a web API, read its JSON response and cope when things go wrong.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Calling a REST API with the `requests` library
- Reading nested JSON responses and sending query parameters
- Handling network errors, timeouts and unexpected data
- Cleaning HTML-encoded text with `html.unescape`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install requests and, in a scratch script, fetch `https://opentdb.com/api.php?amount=5&type=multiple` and print the JSON to understand its shape.
2. Write `fetch_questions(amount, difficulty=None)` in `api.py` that builds the request with the `params=` argument and a `timeout`.
3. Convert each API result into your `Question` class, mixing the correct answer in with the incorrect ones and shuffling the choices.
4. Decode text like `"` and `'` with `html.unescape` before displaying it.
5. Check the API's `response_code` field and handle timeouts, no internet and bad responses with clear messages, falling back to your local decks.
6. Add an `Online quiz` menu option that asks for the number of questions and difficulty, then plays using your existing `QuizSession`.
7. Let the player save an online round as a new deck in `decks.json` so it works offline later.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] An online quiz of 5-10 questions plays correctly with shuffled choices
- [ ] No question shows raw codes like `"`
- [ ] Disconnecting from the internet shows a friendly message and the app keeps working
- [ ] Every request uses a `timeout` value
- [ ] Saved online decks appear in the deck list after a restart

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- The API limits how often one computer can call it, so avoid calling it in a tight loop.
- Call `response.raise_for_status()` inside `try/except requests.RequestException` to catch HTTP errors as well.
- Browse opentdb.com to see which categories and parameters the API accepts.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Fetch the list of categories from the API and let the player choose one before starting an online quiz.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Integrated the free Open Trivia Database API into my Python quiz app
Handled network errors and timeouts with an offline fallback to local decks
Parsed and cleaned JSON API data into my own Question classes

4.title: Web Quiz with Flask and Tests
deliverables: A Flask web app with deck list, quiz, results and stats pages
At least 4 passing pytest tests
`requirements.txt` and an updated README with screenshots
A 30-60 second demo video
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Give QuizCraft a simple web interface with Flask so anyone can play in a browser, and add pytest tests for your core classes. You finish with a polished, documented app and a short demo video.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Building pages with Flask routes and Jinja templates
- Handling forms and keeping quiz state in Flask's `session`
- Writing unit tests with `pytest`
- Documenting a project with a clear README

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install Flask and create `app.py` with a home page that lists your decks and links to an online quiz.
2. Build a `/play/<deck>` route that shows one question at a time in a form, keeping the current question number and score in `session`.
3. Show a results page with the score and the correct answers for any mistakes, and save the result to `progress.json` using your existing code.
4. Add a `/stats` page that shows each player's attempts and best scores.
5. Write at least 4 pytest tests: answer checking with odd spacing and case, multiple-choice checking, loading a deck, and converting an API result from sample JSON.
6. Add basic CSS so the pages look clean and readable on a phone screen.
7. Update the README with setup steps, screenshots, and how to run the app and tests, then record a 30-60 second demo.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] A full quiz can be played in the browser from the first question to the results page
- [ ] Refreshing the page mid-quiz does not reset or double-count the score
- [ ] Results from the web app show up on the stats page
- [ ] `pytest` passes with at least 4 tests and makes no real network calls
- [ ] The app runs locally with `flask --app app run` by following the README

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Flask's `session` needs `app.secret_key` to be set, otherwise you will get an error.
- Return a `redirect(...)` after handling each POST so refreshing the page does not resubmit an answer.
- The [Flask docs](https://flask.palletsprojects.com) quickstart covers routes, templates, forms and sessions.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a countdown timer for each question, or a leaderboard page showing the top 5 scores for each deck.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a Flask web version of my Python quiz and flashcard app
Managed quiz state across pages using Flask sessions and forms
Wrote pytest tests for answer checking and API data conversion

1.title: Product Grid with Components & Props
deliverables: A Vite + React project that runs with `npm run dev`
`Header`, `ProductCard` and `ProductGrid` components in separate files
A styled grid of at least 8 products from a local data file
