1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Set up a React project with Vite and build the store's home page from small, reusable components: a header, a product card and a product grid. You will learn how React breaks a page into pieces and passes data between them.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Creating and running a React project with Vite
- Writing components in JSX
- Passing data to components with props
- Rendering lists with `.map()` and the `key` prop

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Run `npm create vite@latest omnistore -- --template react`, then `npm install` and `npm run dev`, and open the local URL.
2. Delete the Vite demo content in `App.jsx` and `App.css` so you start from a blank page, then commit.
3. Create a `src/data/products.js` file exporting an array of 8-10 product objects with `id`, `title`, `price`, `category` and `image`.
4. Build a `Header` component with the store name and a cart icon showing a fixed number like 0.
5. Build a `ProductCard` component that receives one product as props and shows its image, title, category and price.
6. Build a `ProductGrid` component that maps over the products array and renders a `ProductCard` for each, using `product.id` as the key.
7. Style the grid with CSS Grid so it shows several cards per row, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The app starts with `npm run dev` without errors
- [ ] Each component lives in its own file under `src/components`
- [ ] `ProductCard` gets all its data through props (no hard-coded product text)
- [ ] The browser console shows no 'unique key' warning
- [ ] Adding a product to the data file makes a new card appear

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Component names must start with a capital letter, or React treats them as HTML tags.
- Free product images can come from placeholder services or your own screenshots stored in `public/`.
- Format prices with `price.toLocaleString('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' })`.
- The official tutorial at [react.dev](https://react.dev) explains components and props clearly.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `Footer` component and a small badge on cards for products marked as `onSale`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Set up a React project with Vite and built a product catalogue for an online store
Broke the UI into reusable components and passed data with props
Rendered a dynamic product grid from a data file using map and keys

2.title: Shopping Cart & Search with State
deliverables: Add-to-cart buttons on every product
A cart panel with quantity controls, remove buttons and a live total
A header cart count that updates instantly
A working search box and a demo video of the cart in action
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Make the store interactive by adding a working cart and a search box using React state. You will learn how state makes the UI update automatically and how to share state between components.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Storing changing data with the `useState` hook
- Handling click and input events in React
- Lifting state up to a parent component and passing functions as props
- Calculating derived values like cart totals from state

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. In `App`, create `const [cart, setCart] = useState([])` where each item looks like `{ id, title, price, qty }`.
2. Add an 'Add to cart' button in `ProductCard` that calls an `onAddToCart(product)` function passed down from `App`.
3. In `onAddToCart`, increase `qty` if the product is already in the cart, otherwise add it with `qty: 1`, always creating a new array.
4. Build a `Cart` panel that lists items with + and - buttons, a remove button, and the total price.
5. Show the total item count on the header cart icon using a value calculated from `cart`.
6. Add a search input with its own state and show only products whose title includes the search text.
7. Test adding, changing quantities, removing and searching, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Adding the same product twice increases its quantity instead of adding a duplicate row
- [ ] Reducing quantity to 0 removes the item from the cart
- [ ] The total price and header count are always correct
- [ ] Search filters products as you type and shows a 'No products found' message when nothing matches
- [ ] State is never changed directly (no `cart.push`)

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use `cart.map()` to update one item and `cart.filter()` to remove one, so you always return a new array.
- Do not store the total in state; calculate it with `cart.reduce()` on every render.
- A controlled input uses both `value={search}` and `onChange={e => setSearch(e.target.value)}`.
- Read 'Adding Interactivity' and 'Managing State' on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add category filter buttons that work together with the search box.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a working shopping cart in React using the useState hook
Lifted state up to share cart data between the product grid, header and cart panel
Added live product search with controlled inputs

3.title: Real Products, Detail Pages & Routing
deliverables: A product grid loaded from the DummyJSON API
A product detail page for every product at `/product/:id`
Loading and error messages on both pages
A demo video browsing from the grid to a product and back
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace your local data with real products from the free DummyJSON API and add a separate page for each product using React Router. You will learn how React apps load data and move between pages without reloading.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Fetching data inside `useEffect` and storing it in state
- Showing loading and error states while data loads
- Client-side routing with React Router (`Routes`, `Route`, `Link`)
- Reading URL parameters with `useParams`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Open `https://dummyjson.com/products?limit=30` in your browser to see the data shape (`products`, `title`, `price`, `thumbnail`, `category`).
2. In `App`, fetch the products inside a `useEffect` with an empty dependency array and save them in state, along with `loading` and `error` state.
3. Show a 'Loading products...' message while loading and a friendly error message if the fetch fails.
4. Install React Router with `npm install react-router-dom` and set up routes for `/` (the grid) and `/product/:id` (details).
5. Wrap each product card in a `Link` to its detail page.
6. Build a `ProductDetail` page that reads the id with `useParams`, fetches `https://dummyjson.com/products/<id>`, and shows images, description, rating and an Add to cart button.
7. Add a 404 route for unknown URLs and test navigation with the browser back button.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The home page shows products from the API, not the local file
- [ ] Clicking a card opens its detail page without a full page reload
- [ ] Refreshing on a detail page still shows the correct product
- [ ] A failed request shows an error message instead of a blank screen
- [ ] Visiting an unknown URL shows a Not Found page

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Forgetting the dependency array in `useEffect` causes an infinite fetch loop.
- Check `response.ok` before calling `response.json()` so HTTP errors are caught.
- Your cart from Week 2 still works, as long as API products have an `id`, `title` and `price`.
- See [reactrouter.com](https://reactrouter.com) for setup and the `useParams` hook.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Fetch categories from `https://dummyjson.com/products/categories` and add a category filter.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Connected my React store to the DummyJSON API using useEffect and fetch
Added product detail pages with React Router and URL parameters
Handled loading and error states for a smoother shopping experience

4.title: Global Cart with Context & Checkout
deliverables: A `CartContext` used by every component that needs the cart
A cart that survives a page refresh
A validated checkout form and an order confirmation page
A live URL and a README with screenshots
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Move the cart into React Context so any page can use it, save it in localStorage, and build a practice checkout form with validation. You will finish with a complete, deployed mini store and a clear README.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Sharing state across pages with `createContext` and `useContext`
- Syncing state to `localStorage` with `useEffect`
- Building and validating a controlled form
- Deploying a Vite app to a free host

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a `CartContext` with a `CartProvider` that holds the cart state and the add, remove and update functions.
2. Wrap your app in `CartProvider` and replace the cart props with `useContext(CartContext)` in the header, cards, detail page and cart.
3. Load the initial cart from `localStorage` and save it in a `useEffect` whenever the cart changes.
4. Add a `/checkout` route with a form for name, phone, address and pincode, with an order summary beside it.
5. Validate the form on submit (required fields, 10-digit phone, 6-digit pincode) and show errors next to each field.
6. On success, clear the cart and show an 'Order placed' page with a fake order number (no real payment).
7. Write a README with screenshots and setup steps, then deploy with `npm run build` to Netlify or Vercel's free plan.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] No component receives cart data or functions through props anymore
- [ ] Refreshing the page keeps the cart contents
- [ ] Submitting the checkout with invalid data shows field-level errors
- [ ] A valid order clears the cart and shows a confirmation
- [ ] The deployed app works, including refreshing on a detail page

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Put the context and provider in their own file like `src/context/CartContext.jsx` to keep things tidy.
- Pass a function to `useState` to read localStorage only once: `useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('cart')) || [])`.
- If refreshing a route gives a 404 on Netlify, add a `_redirects` file in `public/` with `/* /index.html 200`.
- Read 'Passing Data Deeply with Context' on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a coupon code field that applies a 10% discount for the code `SKILLME10`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a complete React e-commerce store with a global cart using Context
Persisted the cart with localStorage and added a validated checkout flow
Deployed OmniStore live with product pages, search and cart

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Set up a React project with Vite and build the StreamVibe home page: a navbar, a hero section with a video, and rows of show cards. You will learn how to split a page into reusable components and pass data with props.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Creating and running a React project with Vite
- Writing components in JSX
- Passing data to components with props
- Rendering lists with `.map()` and keys

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Run `npm create vite@latest streamvibe -- --template react`, then `npm install` and `npm run dev`.
2. Clear out the Vite demo code and commit a blank starting point.
3. Create `src/data/shows.js` with 10-12 show objects containing `id`, `title`, `genre`, `year`, `rating` and `poster`.
4. Build a `Navbar` component and a `Hero` component that shows a featured title, a short description and a native `<video controls>` element playing a short sample clip saved in `public/`.
5. Build a `ShowCard` component that receives one show as props and shows its poster, title, year and rating.
6. Build a `ShowRow` component that takes a `title` and a list of shows, and renders them in a horizontal row.
7. In `App`, render two or three `ShowRow`s such as 'Trending' and 'Comedy' by filtering the data, then style with a dark theme and commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The app starts with `npm run dev` without errors
- [ ] `ShowCard` and `ShowRow` get their data only through props
- [ ] The same `ShowRow` component is reused for every row
- [ ] The hero video plays with native controls
- [ ] There are no key warnings in the console

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Keep the sample video short and small (a few MB) so it loads quickly and fits in your repo.
- Use `overflow-x: auto` and `display: flex` on rows to get the sideways-scrolling Netflix look.
- Posters can be any free images you have the right to use, or plain coloured boxes with the title for now.
- Components and props are explained in the tutorial on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a hover effect that slightly enlarges a card and shows its genre.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built the home page of a Netflix-style streaming app with React and Vite
Created reusable ShowCard and ShowRow components driven by props
Added a hero section with a playable video using the HTML video element

2.title: Genre Filters, Details & Watchlist with State
deliverables: Working genre filter buttons
A details modal that opens and closes
A watchlist row with add and remove buttons

2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Make StreamVibe interactive with React state: filter shows by genre, open a details modal, and add shows to a watchlist. You will learn how state and events drive what the user sees.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Storing changing data with `useState`
- Handling click events and passing handler functions as props
- Conditional rendering (showing or hiding a modal)
- Lifting state up so several components share it

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add genre buttons (All, Drama, Comedy, Sci-Fi and so on) and a `selectedGenre` state in `App` that filters the shows shown.
2. Add a `selectedShow` state and make clicking a `ShowCard` set it.
3. Build a `ShowModal` component that appears only when `selectedShow` is not null and shows the full details with a Close button.
4. Add a `watchlist` state in `App` holding show ids, and an 'Add to Watchlist' / 'Remove' toggle button in the modal and on cards.
5. Add a 'My Watchlist' row at the top that shows only shows in the watchlist, or a friendly message when it is empty.
6. Show the watchlist count in the navbar and test every interaction before committing.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Choosing a genre shows only matching shows, and All shows everything
- [ ] Clicking a card opens a modal with that show's details, and Close hides it
- [ ] The watchlist button text changes between Add and Remove correctly
- [ ] A show cannot appear twice in the watchlist
- [ ] The navbar count always matches the watchlist row

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Store only ids in the watchlist and look up full show objects when rendering.
- Use `watchlist.includes(show.id)` to decide which button label to show.
- Close the modal when the dark background is clicked, but stop the click inside the modal with `event.stopPropagation()`.
- See 'Adding Interactivity' on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Let users close the modal with the Escape key.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added genre filtering and a show details modal to my React streaming app
Built a watchlist feature using useState and lifted state
Used conditional rendering and event handlers to create a smooth browsing experience

3.title: Live Shows from the TVMaze API & Routing
deliverables: A home page filled with shows from the TVMaze API
A working search that shows live results

3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace your local data with real TV shows from the free TVMaze API, add live search, and give every show its own page with React Router. You will learn how to load data in React and build a multi-page app.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Fetching data with `fetch` inside `useEffect`
- Handling loading, empty and error states
- Client-side routing with React Router and `useParams`
- Re-running an effect when a value such as a search term changes

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Open `https://api.tvmaze.com/shows` in your browser and note the fields you need: `id`, `name`, `genres`, `image.medium`, `rating.average` and `summary`.
2. Fetch the shows in a `useEffect` in `App`, store them in state, and adapt your components to the new field names.
3. Show a loading message while fetching and an error message if the request fails.
4. Add a search box that calls `https://api.tvmaze.com/search/shows?q=<term>` when the user submits, and shows the results in a row.
5. Install `react-router-dom` and set up routes for `/` and `/show/:id`, linking each card to its page.
6. Build a `ShowPage` that reads the id with `useParams`, fetches `https://api.tvmaze.com/shows/<id>`, and shows the poster, genres, rating, summary and a watchlist button.
7. Test searching for a show, opening it, and using the browser back button.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The home page shows real shows from TVMaze
- [ ] Searching a title shows matching results, and a search with no results shows a message
- [ ] Clicking a show opens its page without a full reload
- [ ] Refreshing a show page still loads the correct show
- [ ] A network failure shows an error message instead of a blank page

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Search results are wrapped: each item looks like `{ score, show }`, so use `item.show`.
- Some shows have no image or rating, so add fallbacks to avoid `Cannot read properties of null` errors.
- The `summary` field contains HTML tags; strip them with `summary.replace(/<[^>]+>/g, '')` before displaying.
- See [reactrouter.com](https://reactrouter.com) for routing basics.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Show the cast on the show page using `https://api.tvmaze.com/shows/<id>/cast`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Connected my React streaming app to the TVMaze API using useEffect and fetch
Added live show search and individual show pages with React Router
Handled loading, empty and error states for real-world API data

4.title: Watchlist with Context, Ratings & Deploy
deliverables: A `WatchlistContext` used across the app
A `/watchlist` page that survives a refresh
A reusable `StarRating` component with saved ratings
A live URL and a README with screenshots
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Move the watchlist into React Context so it works on every page, save it with localStorage, and let users give their own star ratings. Then polish the layout for mobile and deploy StreamVibe for free.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Sharing state across pages with `createContext` and `useContext`
- Persisting state with `localStorage` and `useEffect`
- Building a small reusable interactive component (star rating)
- Building and deploying a Vite app

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a `WatchlistContext` with a provider that holds the watchlist and `add`, `remove` and `isInWatchlist` functions.
2. Replace the watchlist props with `useContext` in cards, the modal and the show page.
3. Store full show objects (id, name, image) in the watchlist so a `/watchlist` page can show them without refetching.
4. Save the watchlist to `localStorage` whenever it changes and load it on startup.
5. Build a `StarRating` component (1-5 clickable stars) and save each user's rating per show id in the same context.
6. Make the layout responsive for phones and write a README with screenshots and setup steps.
7. Run `npm run build` and deploy to Netlify or Vercel's free plan, then test the live link.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The watchlist works on the home page, show pages and watchlist page without prop drilling
- [ ] Watchlist items and ratings are still there after closing and reopening the browser
- [ ] Clicking a star sets the rating and the stars update to show it
- [ ] The app is usable on a phone-sized screen
- [ ] The deployed app loads and routes correctly

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Initialise state from localStorage with a function: `useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('watchlist')) || [])`.
- Render stars with `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map()` and compare each number with the current rating.
- On Netlify, add `public/_redirects` containing `/* /index.html 200` so refreshing deep links works.
- Read 'Passing Data Deeply with Context' on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Build custom play, pause and mute buttons for the hero video using `useRef`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a global watchlist in React using Context and localStorage
Created a reusable star rating component for personal show ratings
Deployed StreamVibe live as a complete React media browsing app

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Set up a React project with Vite and build a page of recipe cards from a local data file. You will learn how to build a UI out of small components that receive data through props.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Creating and running a React project with Vite
- Writing components in JSX
- Passing data with props, including arrays
- Rendering lists with `.map()` and keys

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Run `npm create vite@latest recipebox -- --template react`, then `npm install` and `npm run dev`.
2. Remove the Vite demo code and commit a clean start.
3. Create `src/data/recipes.js` with 6-8 recipes, each with `id`, `name`, `category`, `time` (minutes), `image` and an `ingredients` array.
4. Build a `Header` component with the app name and a short tagline.
5. Build a `RecipeCard` component that shows the image, name, category and cooking time from props.
6. Build an `IngredientList` component that receives the `ingredients` array and renders a `ul`, and use it inside `RecipeCard`.

- [ ] `RecipeCard` shows only data passed in through props
- [ ] `IngredientList` is a separate component used inside each card
- [ ] There are no key warnings in the console
- [ ] Adding a recipe to the data file adds a new card

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Include recipes you actually cook at home, which makes your demo more personal.
- Use `ingredients.map((item, index) => ...)` and prefer a real id over the index when you have one.
- Keep cards the same height by limiting how many ingredients show and adding a 'more...' note.
- Learn the basics in the tutorial at [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a small 'Veg' or 'Non-veg' badge on each card based on a `veg` field.

deliverables: A working search box
Category filter buttons
Favourite toggles and a favourites-only view

2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add interactivity with React state so users can search recipes, filter by category and mark favourites. You will learn how state changes make React update the page for you.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Storing changing values with `useState`
- Controlled inputs for search boxes
- Handling click events and passing handlers as props
- Deriving filtered lists from state instead of storing copies

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add a search input in `App` with `search` state, and show only recipes whose name includes the search text.
2. Add category buttons (All, Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner, Dessert) with a `category` state that works together with search.
3. Add a `favourites` state holding recipe ids, and a heart button on each card that toggles the recipe in or out.
4. Add a 'Show favourites only' toggle that filters the grid to favourite recipes.
5. Show a friendly 'No recipes found' message when the filters match nothing.
6. Test combinations of search, category and favourites, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Search is case-insensitive and updates as you type
- [ ] Category and search filters work at the same time
- [ ] The heart button clearly shows whether a recipe is a favourite
- [ ] The favourites-only toggle shows exactly the favourite recipes
- [ ] An empty result shows a message instead of a blank area

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Compute `visibleRecipes` with `recipes.filter(...)` during render; do not keep it in separate state.
- Toggle a favourite with `favourites.includes(id) ? favourites.filter(f => f !== id) : [...favourites, id]`.
- Highlight the active category button with a conditional class name.
- See 'Managing State' on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'Max cooking time' slider that hides recipes that take longer.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added live search and category filters to my React recipe app
Built a favourites feature with useState and event handlers
Combined multiple filters by deriving data from state

3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Connect RecipeBox to TheMealDB, a free recipe API, so users can search thousands of real dishes and open a detail page for each. You will learn to fetch data in React and build a multi-page app with React Router.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Fetching data with `fetch` inside `useEffect` or an event handler
- Handling loading, empty and error states
- Client-side routing with React Router and `useParams`
- Transforming messy API data into a clean shape

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Try `https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/search.php?s=chicken` in your browser and look at `strMeal`, `strMealThumb`, `strCategory` and `idMeal`.
2. Change the search box to call the API when the form is submitted, and store results, `loading` and `error` in state.
3. Load a default search (for example `s=paneer`) in a `useEffect` when the app first opens.
4. Show 'No recipes found' when the API returns `meals: null`, and a friendly error if the request fails.
5. Install `react-router-dom`, add routes for `/` and `/recipe/:id`, and link each card to its detail page.
6. Build a `RecipePage` that fetches `https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/lookup.php?i=<id>` and shows the image, category, cuisine, instructions and ingredients.
7. Write a helper that turns `strIngredient1..20` and `strMeasure1..20` into a clean array, skipping empty values.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Searching shows real recipes from TheMealDB
- [ ] A search with no matches shows a 'No recipes found' message
- [ ] Clicking a card opens the recipe page without a full reload
- [ ] The recipe page shows a clean ingredient list with no empty rows
- [ ] A network error shows a friendly message

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- The API returns `null` (not an empty array) when nothing is found, so check for it before calling `.map()`.
- Build the ingredient list with a loop from 1 to 20 reading `meal['strIngredient' + i]`.
- Your favourites can keep working if you store `idMeal` values instead of your old ids.
- API details are on [TheMealDB](https://www.themealdb.com) website, and routing on [reactrouter.com](https://reactrouter.com).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'Surprise me' button that loads `random.php` and opens that recipe.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Connected my React recipe app to TheMealDB API for real recipe search
Added recipe detail pages with React Router and URL parameters
Cleaned up messy API data into a readable ingredient list

deliverables: A `PlannerContext` used for favourites and the meal plan

4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Build a weekly meal planner where users add recipes to days of the week, backed by React Context and localStorage. Finish by generating a shopping list, polishing for mobile, and deploying RecipeBox.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Sharing state across pages with `createContext` and `useContext`
- Working with nested state (an object of days holding recipe lists)
- Persisting state with `localStorage`
- Building and deploying a Vite app

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a `PlannerContext` that stores favourites and a `plan` object like `{ Mon: [], Tue: [], ... }`.
2. Move favourites into the context and use `useContext` wherever they are needed.
3. On the recipe page, add a day dropdown and an 'Add to plan' button that saves the recipe's id, name and ingredients to that day.
4. Build a `/planner` page showing the 7 days with their recipes and a remove button on each.
5. Generate a shopping list on the planner page by combining all ingredients from the week and removing duplicates.
6. Save the context data to `localStorage` whenever it changes and load it on startup.
7. Make the planner responsive, write a README with screenshots, then build and deploy to Netlify or Vercel's free plan.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] A recipe can be added to any day and removed again
- [ ] The shopping list updates when the plan changes and has no duplicate ingredients
- [ ] Plans and favourites remain after closing and reopening the browser
- [ ] No component receives planner data through long prop chains
- [ ] The deployed app works on desktop and mobile

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Update nested state with a copy: `setPlan({ ...plan, [day]: [...plan[day], recipe] })`.
- Use a `Set` to remove duplicate ingredient names: `[...new Set(list)]`.
- Add `public/_redirects` with `/* /index.html 200` on Netlify so refreshing `/planner` works.
- Read about Context on [react.dev](https://react.dev).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Let users tick off shopping list items and keep the ticks saved.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.

Generated an automatic shopping list from planned recipes
Deployed RecipeBox live with search, favourites and meal planning

1.title: Tables, Data and Your First Queries
deliverables: `schema.sql` with three tables
`seed.sql` with sample data

README with a screenshot of the tables in DB Browser
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Create a small library database with books, members and loans tables, fill it with sample data and answer simple questions with SELECT. This is the foundation every later week builds on, so getting clean tables now saves time later.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- What tables, rows, columns and data types are
- Writing CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements
- Filtering and sorting with SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY
- Primary keys and why every row needs a unique id

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Install [DB Browser for SQLite](https://sqlitebrowser.org) and create a new database file called `shelfwise.db`.
2. On paper, list the columns you need for `books`, `members` and `loans` before writing any SQL.
3. Write a `schema.sql` file with three `CREATE TABLE` statements, each with an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` column.
4. Write a `seed.sql` file that inserts at least 20 books, 10 members and 25 loans with realistic values.
5. Run both files, then open the Browse Data tab to confirm every row looks correct.
6. Write 8 queries in `queries_week1.sql` using `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` and `LIKE`, each with a comment stating the question it answers.
7. Save the database, SQL files and a short README to a GitHub repo.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Running `schema.sql` then `seed.sql` on an empty database finishes with no errors
- [ ] Each table has a primary key
- [ ] The database contains at least 20 books, 10 members and 25 loans
- [ ] All 8 queries run and return the expected rows

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Store dates as text in `YYYY-MM-DD` format so they sort correctly in SQLite.
- Add `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS` at the top of `schema.sql` so you can re-run it safely.
- The [SQLite documentation](https://sqlite.org/docs.html) lists every data type and keyword.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a `genres` column and write a query that lists all books in one genre sorted by publication year.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.

Wrote CREATE and INSERT scripts to build and seed the database from scratch
Answered 8 practical questions using SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Connect your tables with foreign keys and use JOINs and GROUP BY to answer questions that span several tables. You will also tidy the design so data is not repeated.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Foreign keys and constraints such as NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK
- INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN
- Aggregates with GROUP BY and HAVING
- Basic normalisation: removing repeated data into its own table

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Look for repeated values in `books` (for example author names) and move them into an `authors` table linked by `author_id`.
2. Rewrite `schema.sql` with `FOREIGN KEY` references, `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` on member email and a `CHECK` that return dates come after loan dates.
3. Run `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` and try inserting a loan for a member who does not exist to confirm it is rejected.
4. Write 4 JOIN queries, such as listing each loan with the member name and book title.
5. Write a LEFT JOIN query that finds books that have never been borrowed.
6. Write 4 GROUP BY queries, including one that uses `HAVING` to find members with more than 3 loans.
7. Update the README with a before/after note explaining your normalisation change.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] An `authors` table exists and `books` references it by id
- [ ] Inserting a loan with an invalid member id fails with a foreign key error
- [ ] At least one query uses LEFT JOIN to find unmatched rows
- [ ] At least one query uses HAVING correctly
- [ ] All scripts still run cleanly on an empty database

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- SQLite ignores foreign keys unless you run `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;` on each connection.
- If a JOIN returns far too many rows, you are probably missing a join condition.
- Use WHERE to filter rows before grouping and HAVING to filter groups after.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Support books with multiple authors by adding a `book_authors` linking table and query it with two JOINs.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Normalised a library database and linked tables with foreign keys
Added constraints that block invalid data at the database level
Wrote JOIN and GROUP BY queries to find popular books and active members

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Answer harder questions with subqueries and CTEs, save useful queries as views, and make lookups faster with indexes. You will also learn to read a simple query plan.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Subqueries and Common Table Expressions (WITH)
- Creating and using views
- What an index is and when it helps
- Reading EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output at a basic level

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Increase your data to at least 200 loans using a small script or spreadsheet export so performance differences are visible.
2. Write 3 queries using subqueries, such as members who borrowed more books than the average member.
3. Rewrite one of them as a CTE with `WITH` and compare which version is easier to read.
4. Create two views: `overdue_loans` and `member_activity`, then query them like normal tables.
5. Run `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` on a query that filters loans by member, and note whether it says SCAN or SEARCH.
6. Add an index on `loans(member_id)`, run the plan again and record the change in your README.
7. Write a short note explaining one case where an index is not worth adding.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 3 queries use a subquery and at least 1 uses a CTE
- [ ] Both views exist and return correct rows
- [ ] EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output changes from SCAN to SEARCH after adding the index
- [ ] The database has at least 200 loans

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Build complex queries in small pieces: run the inner query on its own first.
- Views store the query, not the data, so they always show current rows.
- Search 'SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN' to see examples of SCAN versus SEARCH output.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Use a window function like `RANK()` to rank members by number of loans within each month.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Wrote subqueries and CTEs to answer multi-step questions about library usage
Created views to simplify common reports
Added an index and verified the speed-up with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Turn your database into a short analytics report that answers 8-10 real questions a librarian would ask. Finish with an ER diagram, a clean README and a demo.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Framing business questions and answering them with SQL

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write down 8-10 questions a librarian would care about, such as busiest months, most overdue members and least-borrowed genres.
2. Answer each question with one query in `report.sql`, reusing your views where it helps.
3. Draw an ER diagram of your final schema using [dbdiagram.io](https://dbdiagram.io) or [draw.io](https://www.drawio.com) and export it as an image.
4. Create a `REPORT.md` with each question, the query, a screenshot or table of results and a one-line insight.
5. Optionally build a small [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io) page that runs 3-4 of your queries and shows the results as tables or charts.
6. Test the whole project from a fresh clone: build the database from scripts and run the report.
7. Record a 60-second demo walking through the ER diagram and three insights.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The report answers at least 8 distinct questions, each with a working query
- [ ] Each answer includes a one-line plain-English insight
- [ ] The ER diagram matches the actual tables and relationships
- [ ] Someone can rebuild the database from the README instructions alone

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Good questions start with 'which', 'how many' or 'what share'; avoid questions a single SELECT * can answer.
- Keep your report short and scannable: question, query, result, insight.
- If you use Streamlit, `sqlite3` from the Python standard library is enough to run queries.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a fines table and a query that calculates the total fine each member owes for overdue books.

### 📤 Submission

- Generate realistic sample rows in a spreadsheet and export them as CSV if typing gets slow.

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Split orders into orders and order items so one order can hold many products, then use JOINs and GROUP BY to calculate revenue. This is how real shop databases are structured.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- One-to-many relationships and foreign keys
- Normalisation into orders and order_items
- INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN across three tables
- SUM, COUNT, AVG with GROUP BY and HAVING

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create an `order_items` table with `order_id`, `product_id`, `quantity` and `unit_price`, and move product details out of `orders`.
2. Add `FOREIGN KEY`, `NOT NULL` and a `CHECK (quantity > 0)` constraint, then test that bad inserts are rejected.
3. Reseed the data so most orders contain 1-4 items.
4. Write a query that joins orders, order items, products and customers into one readable list.
5. Calculate total revenue per category and per month with GROUP BY.
6. Use HAVING to list customers who spent more than a chosen amount.
7. Use a LEFT JOIN to find products that have never been ordered.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] One order can contain multiple products through `order_items`
- [ ] A negative or zero quantity is rejected by a CHECK constraint
- [ ] Revenue per category is calculated from order items, not typed in
- [ ] At least one query uses LEFT JOIN and one uses HAVING

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Store `unit_price` in `order_items` because product prices can change later.
- To group by month in SQLite use `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)`; in PostgreSQL use `date_trunc('month', order_date)`.
- Check your totals by hand for one order to confirm the JOIN is correct.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Calculate average order value per customer city and sort cities from highest to lowest.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Normalised an e-commerce schema into orders and order items
Used JOINs and GROUP BY to calculate revenue by category and month
Enforced data quality with foreign keys and CHECK constraints

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Compute stats like strike rate and economy using CTEs and subqueries, save them as views and speed up common queries with indexes. Ball-by-ball data is large, so indexes make a visible difference.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Subqueries and CTEs
- Views for reusable stat tables
- Indexes and EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
- Avoiding integer division and divide-by-zero errors

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write a CTE that calculates runs and balls faced per batter, then compute strike rate from it.
2. Write a query for bowler economy rate and handle bowlers with zero overs safely.
3. Use a subquery to find batters whose strike rate is above the overall average.
4. Create views `batting_summary` and `bowling_summary`.
5. Time a query filtering deliveries by `match_id`, check `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, add an index and compare.
6. Record query times and plans before and after in your README.

- [ ] Strike rate and economy are calculated correctly for at least 5 players you check by hand
- [ ] No query fails or returns wrong values because of division by zero
- [ ] Both views return correct results
- [ ] The query plan shows an index in use after you add it

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Strike rate is runs divided by balls, times 100; multiply by `1.0` to avoid integer division.
- Use `NULLIF(balls, 0)` so division by zero returns NULL instead of an error.
- DB Browser shows execution time under the query results.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Rank the top 3 run-scorers for each season using `ROW_NUMBER()` in a CTE.

### 📤 Submission

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Talk to real students about canteen queues, turn what you hear into a persona and a clear problem statement, and map the ordering flow. Good design starts with understanding people, not with screens.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Planning and running short user interviews
- Creating a persona from real findings
- Writing a problem statement
- Mapping a simple user flow

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write 6-8 open-ended interview questions, such as 'Tell me about the last time you bought food at the canteen.'
2. Interview 3-5 students for 10 minutes each, or run a short Google Form survey with at least 15 responses.
3. Write each finding on a sticky note in a [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) board and group similar notes together.
4. Create one persona with a name, goals, frustrations and a quote taken from your research.
5. Write a problem statement in the form 'Students need a way to ___ because ___.'
6. Draw a user flow from opening the app to picking up the order, including one alternate path such as an item being sold out.
7. Share the FigJam link and write a short summary of your top 3 insights.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
- [ ] Findings are grouped into at least 3 themes
- [ ] The persona includes goals, frustrations and a real quote
- [ ] The user flow covers the full order journey plus one alternate path

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Ask about past behaviour, not opinions; 'What did you do?' is better than 'Would you use...?'
- Avoid leading questions such as 'Don't you hate long queues?'
- Keep the persona based on what you heard, not on guesses.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Visit the canteen at peak time, time the queue and add these observations to your research.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Interviewed students to understand canteen queue problems
Created a research-based persona and problem statement
Mapped the full pre-order user flow in FigJam

2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Turn your user flow into grayscale wireframes for the main screens. Wireframes let you test layout and flow quickly before spending time on colours and details.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Information hierarchy and layout
- Using frames and basic shapes in Figma
- Sketching multiple ideas before choosing one
- Linking wireframes to the user flow

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Sketch 2-3 paper versions of the menu screen and pick the one that best solves your problem statement.
2. In [Figma](https://www.figma.com), create a mobile frame and build wireframes for: home, menu, item details, cart, checkout and order status.
3. Use only gray boxes, simple text and placeholder icons; no colours or images yet.
4. Place the most important action on each screen where the thumb can reach it easily.
5. Arrange the screens left to right in flow order and label each one.
6. Show the wireframes to one classmate and note anything that confused them.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 6 screens cover the full flow from Week 1
- [ ] Each screen has one clear primary action
- [ ] Screens are in grayscale with no final visual styling
- [ ] At least one change was made based on feedback

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use Figma's mobile frame presets so your screens have realistic sizes.
- Real content labels such as 'Masala Dosa - Rs 40' reveal layout problems better than 'Lorem ipsum'.
- Search 'low fidelity wireframe examples' for reference before starting.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add wireframes for an empty cart and an item-sold-out state.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Sketched and compared multiple layout ideas on paper
Built 6 low-fidelity wireframes in Figma for a canteen pre-order app
Improved the flow based on early feedback

3.title: High-fidelity UI and Mini Design System
deliverables: Design System page with colours, type and components
At least 6 high-fidelity screens
Screenshot of contrast checks
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Create a small design system with colours, a type scale and reusable components, then use it to turn your wireframes into polished screens. You will also check basic accessibility.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Colour styles and text styles
- Reusable components and variants
- Auto layout for flexible buttons and cards
- Basic accessibility: colour contrast and tap target size

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Pick a primary colour, a neutral palette and one accent, and save them as colour styles.
2. Define a type scale of 4-5 sizes (for example 12, 14, 16, 20, 28) and save them as text styles.
3. Build components with auto layout: button, menu item card, input field, and bottom navigation.
4. Add button variants for default, pressed and disabled states.
5. Rebuild all 6 screens using only your styles and components.
6. Check text contrast with a Figma contrast plugin and make tap targets at least 44x44 pt.
7. Create a 'Design System' page in the file that shows all styles and components.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] All colours and text on screens use saved styles
- [ ] At least 4 reusable components exist, one with variants
- [ ] Buttons and cards use auto layout
- [ ] Body text meets a 4.5:1 contrast ratio
- [ ] Tap targets are at least 44x44 pt

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Change a component's main copy and confirm every instance updates; if not, you detached it.
- Use an 8-point spacing system (8, 16, 24, 32) for consistent layouts.
- The [WCAG overview from W3C](https://www.w3.org/WAI/) explains contrast requirements.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Create a dark mode version of two screens using the same components.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a mini design system with colour styles, a type scale and components
Designed 6 high-fidelity screens using auto layout
Checked colour contrast and tap target sizes for accessibility

4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Link your screens into a clickable prototype, test it with 3 people, fix the biggest issues and write a case study. This shows your full process from research to tested design.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Prototyping with interactions in Figma
- Running a simple usability test
- Prioritising and fixing issues
- Writing a UX case study

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Connect all screens in Figma's Prototype tab so a user can place an order from start to finish.
2. Write 3 tasks for testers, such as 'Order a dosa and a tea for pickup at 1 pm.'
3. Test with 3 people, ask them to think aloud and note where they hesitate or make mistakes.
4. List all issues, rank them by how many testers hit them and fix the top 3.
5. Write a case study on Notion, Medium or Behance covering problem, research, wireframes, UI, testing and changes.
6. Record a 60-second screen video of the final prototype.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] A tester can complete an order in the prototype without help
- [ ] 3 usability tests are documented with issues found
- [ ] At least 3 issues are fixed and shown before and after
- [ ] The case study covers every stage from research to testing

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- During testing, stay quiet and let the tester struggle a little; that is where the insights are.
- Use 'Smart animate' sparingly; clear flows matter more than fancy transitions.
- Start the case study with the problem and the result, then show the process.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Measure task completion time for each tester before and after your fixes.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built a clickable Figma prototype for a canteen pre-order app
Ran usability tests with 3 students and fixed the top issues
Published a full UX case study from research to tested design

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Research why students start and abandon habits, then create a persona, problem statement and user flow. This keeps your design focused on real needs instead of adding every feature you can think of.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Writing unbiased research questions
- Running interviews or a survey
- Personas and problem statements
- User flows

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write 6-8 open-ended questions about habits students have tried and why they stopped.
2. Interview 3-5 people or collect at least 15 survey responses.
3. Group findings into themes on a [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) board.
4. Look at 2 existing habit apps and note one thing each does well and one thing that frustrates users.
5. Create a persona and write a problem statement based on your strongest theme.
6. Draw a user flow for adding a new habit and checking it off each day.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
- [ ] Findings are grouped into at least 3 themes
- [ ] The problem statement is based on a research theme
- [ ] The user flow covers adding and completing a habit

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Ask 'Tell me about the last habit you tried to build' to get real stories.
- Competitor reviews on app stores are a free source of user frustrations.
- Pick one core problem; a focused app is easier to design well.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Create a second persona with a different motivation and note how their flow differs.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Researched why students struggle to keep habits
Reviewed existing habit apps to find gaps
Created a persona, problem statement and user flow in FigJam

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Create grayscale wireframes for the main screens of your habit tracker. Focus on making adding and checking off a habit fast and obvious.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Visual hierarchy
- Frames, shapes and grids in Figma
- Designing for one-handed mobile use
- Getting quick feedback on layouts

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Sketch 2-3 paper versions of the home screen showing today's habits.
2. In [Figma](https://www.figma.com), build wireframes for: onboarding, home, add habit, habit details and weekly progress.
3. Keep everything grayscale and use real labels like 'Drink 8 glasses of water'.
4. Make checking off a habit possible with a single tap on the home screen.
5. Arrange screens in flow order with labels.
6. Get feedback from one person and write down what you changed.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 5 screens cover the flow from Week 1
- [ ] A habit can be checked off in one tap on the home screen
- [ ] Screens are grayscale with no final styling
- [ ] At least one change was made from feedback

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use a layout grid on your frames to keep spacing consistent.
- Keep onboarding to 3 screens or fewer.
- If you cannot explain a screen's purpose in one sentence, simplify it.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Wireframe an empty state for a new user with no habits yet.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Explored multiple home screen layouts through paper sketches
Wireframed 5 core screens for a habit tracker in Figma
Designed one-tap habit check-off based on user needs

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Define a small design system and apply it to create high-fidelity screens. You will learn how components and styles keep a design consistent and easy to update.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Colour and text styles
- Components with variants
- Auto layout

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Choose a calm colour palette and save primary, neutral, success and error colours as styles.
2. Set up a type scale of 4-5 text styles.
3. Build components with auto layout: habit row, checkbox, button, progress ring or bar, and tab bar.
4. Add variants for the habit row: not done, done and missed.
5. Rebuild all wireframe screens using your components.
6. Check contrast and make sure tap targets are at least 44x44 pt.
7. Document everything on a 'Design System' page.

### ✅ Done When

- [ ] The habit row component has at least 3 variants
- [ ] Buttons and rows use auto layout

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Do not rely on colour alone to show 'done'; add a checkmark icon too.
- Use an 8-point spacing system.
- Name layers and components clearly so your file is easy to share.

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Pick a local business with an outdated website, audit what is not working and talk to people who might use it. A redesign is only useful if you know which problems to fix.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Running a heuristic review of an existing site
- User interviews or surveys
- Personas and problem statements
- Mapping the current user journey

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Choose a local clinic, coaching centre, cafe or shop whose website you find hard to use.
2. Take screenshots of the key pages and mark problems such as unclear navigation, small text or missing contact details.
3. Rate the site against 5 of Nielsen's usability heuristics and note one example for each.
4. Interview 3 people or survey at least 15 about what they look for on such a website.
5. Create a persona and a problem statement.
6. Draw a user flow for the most common task, such as booking an appointment or finding opening hours.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] At least 5 issues are identified on the current site
- [ ] At least 3 interviews or 15 survey responses are recorded
- [ ] The problem statement links to your findings
- [ ] The user flow covers one complete task

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Search 'Nielsen 10 usability heuristics' for the list and examples.
- Pick a site with clear room for improvement but not so large that the project gets out of hand.
- This is a practice redesign; mention in your case study that it is an unofficial concept.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Time how long 2 people take to find a key piece of information on the current site.

### 📤 Submission
No code needed. Set your Figma file's share access to **Anyone with the link can view**, then share a LinkedIn post with 2–4 screens (or a 30–60 second prototype walkthrough), a line on the problem you're solving and the Figma link, and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Audited a local business website using usability heuristics
Interviewed potential users to understand their needs
Defined a persona, problem statement and user flow for the redesign

### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same Figma file.

Reorganise the site's content into a clear structure and create grayscale wireframes for desktop and mobile. Good structure is the biggest improvement in most redesigns.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Information architecture and sitemaps
- Wireframing for desktop and mobile
- Content hierarchy
- Responsive layout basics

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. List every piece of content on the current site and group it into logical pages.
2. Draw a new sitemap in [FigJam](https://www.figma.com) with no more than 5-6 top-level pages.
3. Wireframe the home page, the main task page and a contact page for desktop.
4. Create mobile versions of the same 3 pages.
5. Make the main task, such as 'Book appointment', reachable from the home page in one click.
6. Get feedback from one person and note your changes.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The sitemap has no more than 6 top-level pages
- [ ] Desktop and mobile wireframes exist for 3 pages
- [ ] The main task is one click from the home page
- [ ] At least one change was made from feedback

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use the words your interviewees used as navigation labels.
- Design mobile first if most users will visit on their phones.
- Keep wireframes grayscale so feedback focuses on structure.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Run a quick card-sorting exercise with 2 people to validate your navigation groups.

### 📤 Submission

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Prototype the main task flow on mobile, such as booking an appointment.
2. Ask 3 people to do the same task on the old site and your prototype, and note time and problems.
3. Fix the top 3 issues found in your prototype.

5. Label the project clearly as an unofficial concept redesign.
6. Record a 60-second walkthrough of the new flow.

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Give testers the same task wording for both versions to keep the comparison fair.
- Report simple numbers like average time or number of errors.

1.title: Your First Portfolio Page with HTML & CSS
deliverables: An `index.html` and `style.css` portfolio page with About, Projects and Contact sections
At least 3 styled project cards
A Git repository with at least 3 meaningful commits

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Build a single-page portfolio with a header, an About section, a Projects section and a Contact section using only HTML and CSS. This is the base you will keep improving every week, so focus on clean structure and simple, readable styling.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Semantic HTML tags like `header`, `nav`, `main`, `section` and `footer`
- The CSS box model: margin, border, padding and content
- Flexbox for laying out a navbar and rows of cards
- Using CSS variables for colours and fonts so the design stays consistent

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a folder with `index.html`, `style.css` and an `images/` folder, then run `git init` and make your first commit.
2. Write the HTML skeleton first with no styling: a `nav` with links, then `section` blocks with ids `about`, `projects` and `contact`.
3. Fill in real content: a short bio, a profile photo, and 3 project cards (title, one-line description, and a link, even if it is just `#` for now).
4. Link `style.css` and define 3-4 colours and a font in `:root` as CSS variables.
5. Style the navbar with flexbox so the links sit in a row, and make the nav links jump to each section using `href="#about"` style anchors.
6. Style the project cards as a flex row with `gap`, padding, a border radius and a light shadow.
7. Open the page in your browser, check every section, and commit your work with a clear message.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The page uses semantic tags (`header`, `nav`, `main`, `section`, `footer`) instead of only `div`s
- [ ] Clicking each nav link scrolls to the matching section
- [ ] Colours and fonts are defined once as CSS variables and reused
- [ ] Every image has a meaningful `alt` attribute
- [ ] The page has no broken images or console errors

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Build the HTML completely before writing any CSS, because it is much easier to style a finished structure.
- If spacing looks wrong, use your browser DevTools (right-click, Inspect) to see the box model of each element.
- Add `html { scroll-behavior: smooth; }` for smooth scrolling between sections.
- Look up any tag or CSS property on [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a simple hover effect on project cards (a small lift with `transform: translateY(-4px)` and a `transition`).

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Built my personal portfolio website from scratch using semantic HTML and CSS
Designed a clean layout with flexbox and a consistent colour theme using CSS variables
Structured the page into About, Projects and Contact sections with smooth in-page navigation

deliverables: A portfolio that works on mobile, tablet and desktop widths

2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Make your portfolio look good on phones and start using JavaScript to control the page. You will add a mobile menu and generate your project cards from a JavaScript array, so adding a new project means editing data instead of copying HTML.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Media queries and a mobile-first approach to responsive design
- Selecting elements and listening for events with `querySelector` and `addEventListener`
- Storing data in an array of objects and rendering it to the page with a loop
- Toggling CSS classes from JavaScript to show and hide things

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Open DevTools device mode and check your page at 375px wide to see what breaks.
2. Add media queries so project cards stack in one column on small screens and sit in a row on larger ones.
3. Create `script.js`, link it at the end of `body` (or with `defer`), and log a message to confirm it runs.
4. Add a hamburger button that shows only on mobile, and make clicking it toggle an `open` class on the nav.
5. Move your project data into a `projects` array of objects with `title`, `description`, `tags` and `link` fields.
6. Delete the hard-coded project cards from HTML and write a `renderProjects()` function that builds the cards from the array.
7. Add filter buttons (for example All, HTML/CSS, JavaScript) that re-render only the projects with the matching tag.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] There is no horizontal scrolling at 375px width
- [ ] The hamburger menu opens and closes on small screens and is hidden on desktop
- [ ] Adding a new object to the `projects` array makes a new card appear without touching HTML
- [ ] Clicking a filter button shows only matching projects, and All shows every project
- [ ] The browser console shows no errors

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Add `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` in the `head` or your media queries will not behave as expected on phones.
- Build the cards with template literals and set `container.innerHTML`, clearing the container before each render.
- Use `array.filter()` to pick matching projects and `array.map()` or `forEach` to build the cards.
- Search 'mobile first media queries' on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org) if you are unsure where to start.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Highlight the active filter button and close the mobile menu automatically when a nav link is clicked.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Made my portfolio fully responsive using media queries and a mobile-first approach
Built a mobile hamburger menu with vanilla JavaScript and DOM events
Rendered project cards dynamically from a JavaScript array with category filters

3.title: Live GitHub Repos & Dark Mode
deliverables: A GitHub Repos section populated live from the GitHub REST API
Visible loading and error states for the repos section
A dark mode toggle that is remembered after a page refresh
A demo video showing repos loading and the theme switching
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Connect your portfolio to real data by fetching your public repositories from the GitHub API and showing them on the page. You will also add a dark mode toggle that remembers the visitor's choice using localStorage.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Fetching data from a public API with `fetch` and `async`/`await`
- Handling loading and error states so the page never looks broken
- Saving and reading small settings with `localStorage`
- Theming a site by swapping CSS variables with a class on `body`

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Open `https://api.github.com/users/<your-username>/repos` in your browser to see the JSON you will work with.
2. Add a new 'My GitHub Repos' section with an empty container and a 'Loading...' message.
3. Write an `async function loadRepos()` that fetches the URL, checks `response.ok`, and converts the result with `response.json()`.
4. Render each repo as a small card showing name, description, main language, star count and a link to the repo.
5. Wrap the fetch in `try`/`catch` and show a friendly error message in the section if it fails (test this by breaking the URL on purpose).
6. Add a dark theme by defining a `.dark` class on `body` that overrides your CSS colour variables.
7. Add a theme toggle button that switches the class and saves `'dark'` or `'light'` in `localStorage`, then apply the saved theme when the page loads.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The repos section shows at least 5 of your real public repositories
- [ ] A 'Loading...' message appears before data arrives and is removed afterwards
- [ ] If the fetch fails, a readable error message is shown instead of a blank section
- [ ] Refreshing the page keeps the theme the visitor last selected
- [ ] Both themes are readable with good text contrast

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- The GitHub API allows about 60 unauthenticated requests per hour, so avoid refreshing in a loop while testing.
- Repos with no description return `null`, so show a fallback like 'No description yet'.
- Sort repos by `stargazers_count` or `updated_at` with `array.sort()` before rendering to show your best work first.
- Read about the Fetch API and Window.localStorage on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a language filter dropdown built from the unique `language` values in your repos.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Integrated the GitHub REST API into my portfolio using fetch and async/await
Added loading and error handling so the page stays friendly when the network fails
Built a dark mode toggle that remembers the user's preference with localStorage

4.title: Contact Form, Accessibility & Going Live
deliverables: A contact form with client-side validation and clear error messages
A Lighthouse report screenshot with an accessibility score of 90 or higher
A public live URL for your portfolio
A README with a screenshot, live link and feature list
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Finish your portfolio with a validated contact form, fix accessibility issues, and deploy it for free so anyone can visit it. By the end you will have a real link to put on your resume and LinkedIn profile.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Client-side form validation with JavaScript and helpful error messages
- Basic accessibility: labels, keyboard navigation, focus styles and colour contrast
- Auditing a page with Lighthouse and fixing what it reports
- Deploying a static site to GitHub Pages or Netlify

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Build a contact form with name, email and message fields, each with a proper `label`.
2. On submit, call `event.preventDefault()`, check each field (not empty, valid email format, message at least 20 characters) and show an error next to any invalid field.
3. When the form is valid, show a success message and reset the form (a real email backend is not needed).
4. Navigate the whole page using only the Tab and Enter keys, and add visible `:focus` styles wherever focus is hard to see.
5. Run a Lighthouse audit in Chrome DevTools and fix at least the accessibility and SEO issues it lists (page title, meta description, alt text, contrast).
6. Write a `README.md` with a screenshot, the live link, the features, and what you learned.
7. Push to GitHub and deploy with GitHub Pages (Settings, Pages) or by dragging the folder into Netlify, then test the live link on your phone.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Submitting the form with empty or invalid fields shows specific error messages and does not reset the form
- [ ] Every interactive element can be reached and used with the keyboard alone
- [ ] Lighthouse accessibility score is 90 or above
- [ ] The live URL loads correctly on both desktop and mobile
- [ ] The README includes the live link and at least one screenshot

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Use `aria-live="polite"` on the message area so screen readers announce form errors and success.
- On GitHub Pages, file names are case-sensitive, so `Images/me.png` and `images/me.png` are different.
- Check contrast with the colour picker in DevTools, which shows a contrast ratio for text.
- See [GitHub Pages](https://pages.github.com) for the free hosting setup steps.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Connect the form to a free form service like Formspree so messages actually reach your inbox.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Deployed my personal portfolio live and shared it as my online resume
Built a contact form with client-side validation and accessible error messages
Improved accessibility to a 90+ Lighthouse score with keyboard support and better contrast
