1.title: Kanban Board Layout with HTML & CSS
deliverables: A static Kanban board with three labelled columns
At least 5 styled sample task cards with priority labels
An add-task form in the header (not functional yet)
A screenshot or short video of the board
1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Build the static layout of a Kanban board with three columns and a few sample task cards using HTML and CSS. Getting the structure and look right now makes adding JavaScript next week much easier.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Structuring a page with semantic HTML and sensible class names
- CSS Grid or Flexbox for side-by-side columns
- Styling reusable components (a task card) with one set of CSS rules
- Using CSS variables for colours such as priority labels

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create `index.html`, `style.css` and `script.js` in a new folder, run `git init` and commit.
2. Add a header with the app name and a simple 'Add task' form (a text input, a priority `select` and a button) that does nothing yet.
3. Create a board with three columns: To Do, In Progress and Done, each with a heading and a task count like `(3)`.
4. Inside the columns, hard-code 5-6 sample task cards with a title, a priority label (Low, Medium, High) and a due date.
5. Use CSS Grid (`grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr)`) or Flexbox to put the columns side by side.
6. Style priority labels with different colours using CSS variables and a class such as `.priority-high`.
7. Check the layout in the browser, fix spacing with DevTools, and commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The three columns appear side by side on a laptop screen
- [ ] All task cards share the same CSS class and look consistent
- [ ] High, Medium and Low priorities are visually different
- [ ] The HTML has a clear structure with no inline styles

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Give columns a `min-height` so an empty column still looks like a drop area.
- Keep class names simple and predictable, like `.column`, `.task-card` and `.task-title`, because JavaScript will use them next week.
- Use the DevTools Grid or Flex badge to visualise your layout.
- CSS Grid and Flexbox guides are on [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Make the columns stack vertically on screens narrower than 700px using a media query.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Designed and built the layout for a Kanban task board using HTML and CSS Grid
Created reusable task card styles with colour-coded priority labels
Set up the project structure and Git repository for a browser-based productivity app

2.title: Add, Move & Delete Tasks with JavaScript
deliverables: A working add-task form
Move-left, move-right and delete buttons on every card
Column counts that update automatically
A demo video adding a task and moving it to Done
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Bring the board to life with JavaScript so users can add tasks, move them between columns and delete them. You will learn the key idea of keeping your data in an array and redrawing the page from it.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Keeping app data in an array of objects as the single source of truth
- Handling form submit and click events with `addEventListener`
- Writing a `render()` function that rebuilds the board from data
- Using event delegation to handle clicks on dynamically created buttons

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Remove the hard-coded cards from the HTML and create a `tasks` array in `script.js` with a few sample objects like `{ id, title, priority, status }`.
2. Write `render()`, which clears each column and adds a card for every task whose `status` matches that column.
3. Update the column counts inside `render()` so they always match the data.
4. Handle the add-task form submit: prevent the page reload, ignore empty titles, push a new task with `status: 'todo'` and call `render()`.
5. Add small buttons on each card to move it left or right, and a delete button that asks `confirm()` before removing it.
6. Use one click listener on the board and check `event.target` and a `data-id` attribute to know which task and which button was clicked.
7. Test every action (add, move both ways, delete) and commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Submitting the form adds a new card to To Do without reloading the page
- [ ] Empty task titles are rejected
- [ ] Tasks can be moved between all three columns in both directions
- [ ] Deleting a task removes it after confirmation
- [ ] Column counts always match the number of visible cards

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Never edit the cards directly; change the `tasks` array and then call `render()`.
- Use `Date.now()` as a quick unique id for new tasks.
- Store the order of statuses in an array like `['todo', 'doing', 'done']` so moving is just changing the index.
- Read about event delegation and `dataset` on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Let users edit a task title by double-clicking it.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Made my Kanban board interactive with vanilla JavaScript and DOM events
Implemented adding, moving and deleting tasks from a single data array
Used event delegation to handle clicks on dynamically created task cards

3.title: Saving Tasks & Importing Starter Data
deliverables: Tasks that survive a page refresh
An import button that loads sample tasks from JSONPlaceholder
A live search box that filters task cards
A demo video showing a refresh, an import and a search
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Make your board remember tasks after a refresh with localStorage, and let first-time users import sample tasks from a public API. You will also add search so larger boards stay easy to use.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Saving and loading data with `localStorage`, `JSON.stringify` and `JSON.parse`
- Fetching data from a public API with `fetch` and `async`/`await`
- Handling errors and loading states with `try`/`catch`
- Filtering data live as the user types

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Write `saveTasks()` that stores the `tasks` array in `localStorage`, and call it after every change.
2. On page load, read saved tasks with `JSON.parse`, falling back to an empty array if nothing is saved.
3. Add an 'Import sample tasks' button that fetches `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5`.
4. Convert each API item into your task shape (use `title`, set `status` to `done` if `completed` is true, otherwise `todo`).
5. Show 'Importing...' while loading and a friendly error message if the request fails, using `try`/`catch`.
6. Add a search input that filters visible cards by title as the user types, without changing the saved data.
7. Test by refreshing the page, importing tasks, and turning off Wi-Fi to check the error message.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Adding, moving or deleting a task and then refreshing keeps the change
- [ ] The import button adds 5 tasks placed in the correct columns
- [ ] A clear error message appears if the import fails
- [ ] Typing in the search box shows only matching cards and clearing it shows all cards again
- [ ] The app does not crash if localStorage is empty

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- `localStorage` only stores strings, so always use `JSON.stringify` to save and `JSON.parse` to load.
- Check saved data in DevTools under Application, Local Storage.
- Compare text with `.toLowerCase().includes()` so search is not case-sensitive.
- The Fetch API and Web Storage API are documented on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'Clear board' button and a filter dropdown to show only one priority level.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Added persistence to my Kanban board using localStorage and JSON
Integrated the JSONPlaceholder API to import starter tasks with error handling
Built a live search filter that updates task cards as the user types

4.title: Drag-and-Drop, Polish & Deploy
deliverables: Drag-and-drop between all three columns
A responsive, keyboard-usable board
A public live URL
A README with a screenshot, live link and feature list
4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Add drag-and-drop so tasks can be moved with the mouse, make the board responsive and accessible, and deploy it for free. This is the capstone that turns your board into a portfolio-ready app.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- The HTML Drag and Drop API (`draggable`, `dragstart`, `dragover`, `drop`)
- Keeping a keyboard-friendly alternative for mouse-only features
- Making a multi-column layout responsive
- Deploying a static site to GitHub Pages or Netlify

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add `draggable="true"` to each card and store the task id in `event.dataTransfer` on `dragstart`.
2. On each column, call `event.preventDefault()` in `dragover` so dropping is allowed, and add a highlight class while a card is over it.
3. On `drop`, read the id, update that task's `status`, save and re-render.
4. Keep the move buttons from Week 2 so keyboard users can still move tasks, and add clear `:focus` styles.
5. Add a media query so columns stack on phones, and check the board at 375px.
6. Write a `README.md` with a screenshot or GIF, the live link, the features, and how to run it.
7. Deploy to GitHub Pages or Netlify and test the live version on your phone.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Dragging a card to another column moves it and the change survives a refresh
- [ ] The target column is visibly highlighted while dragging over it
- [ ] Tasks can still be moved using only the keyboard
- [ ] The board is usable on a phone-sized screen
- [ ] The live URL works and is linked in the README

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If `drop` never fires, you probably forgot `event.preventDefault()` in the `dragover` handler.
- Remove the highlight class on both `dragleave` and `drop` so it does not get stuck.
- Native drag-and-drop does not work on most phones, which is another reason to keep the move buttons.
- Search 'HTML Drag and Drop API' on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org) for a full example.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Show a warning colour on cards whose due date has passed, and a small progress bar showing the percentage of tasks in Done.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Implemented drag-and-drop task movement using the native HTML Drag and Drop API
Made my Kanban board responsive and keyboard accessible
Deployed TaskFlow live as a complete vanilla JavaScript productivity app

deliverables: A static weather dashboard page with sample data

1.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
Design and build the static layout of your weather app: a search bar, a large current-weather card and a row of forecast cards, filled with sample data. A clean layout now makes it easy to plug in real data later.

**Level:** Beginner · **Estimated time:** 6-8 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Planning a UI with a quick sketch before coding
- Semantic HTML for forms, headings and sections
- Flexbox for card rows and centred layouts
- Consistent spacing and colours with CSS variables

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Sketch the layout on paper: search bar at the top, a big 'current weather' card, then 7 small forecast cards.
2. Create `index.html`, `style.css` and `script.js`, run `git init` and commit.
3. Build the search form with a text input, a label and a Search button.
4. Build the current-weather card with sample values: city name, temperature, a weather emoji or icon, wind speed and humidity.
5. Build a row of 7 forecast cards with a day name, an icon, and max/min temperatures.
6. Style everything with flexbox and CSS variables, using a calm colour palette and readable font sizes.
7. Review the page in the browser, tidy the spacing, and commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] The search form has a visible label or `aria-label` for the input
- [ ] The current-weather card clearly shows city, temperature and conditions
- [ ] All 7 forecast cards share one CSS class and look consistent
- [ ] There are no inline styles in the HTML

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- Emojis like ☀️, ☁️ and 🌧️ make great free weather icons and need no image files.
- Use `gap` on flex containers instead of adding margins to every card.
- Keep class names clear, such as `.current-temp` and `.forecast-card`, because JavaScript will fill them in later.
- Look up any HTML or CSS feature on [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Make the forecast row scroll horizontally on small screens with `overflow-x: auto`.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.

Created reusable forecast card components with flexbox
Planned the UI with a sketch before writing code

2.title: Rendering Weather Data with JavaScript
deliverables: Current weather and forecast cards rendered entirely from JavaScript data
A working °C/°F toggle
A search form that updates the displayed city name
A demo video switching units and searching
2.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 1 work — keep working in the same repo.

Replace the hard-coded HTML with JavaScript that renders the dashboard from data objects, and add a Celsius/Fahrenheit toggle. This teaches you to separate data from display, which is exactly what you need before using a real API.

**Level:** Beginner+ · **Estimated time:** 8-10 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Representing app data as JavaScript objects and arrays
- Rendering HTML from data with template literals
- Handling form and button events
- Writing small helper functions such as unit conversion

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Create a `sampleWeather` object in `script.js` with a `current` object and a `daily` array of 7 days.
2. Write `renderCurrent(data)` and `renderForecast(days)` functions that fill the cards from the data.
3. Remove the hard-coded forecast cards from the HTML so only JavaScript creates them.
4. Write a `getWeatherEmoji(condition)` helper that returns an emoji for values like 'sunny', 'cloudy' and 'rain'.
5. Add a °C/°F toggle button with a `unit` variable, a `toFahrenheit(c)` helper, and a re-render when the unit changes.
6. Handle the search form submit: prevent the reload, read the input, reject empty values, and show the typed city name on the card for now.
7. Test the toggle and the search form, then commit.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Changing a value in `sampleWeather` changes what the page shows after a refresh
- [ ] The forecast cards are created by JavaScript, not written in HTML
- [ ] The unit toggle converts every temperature on the page correctly
- [ ] Submitting an empty search shows a message instead of doing nothing

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- The conversion is `F = C * 9 / 5 + 32`; round with `Math.round()` for display.
- Always store temperatures in Celsius and convert only when rendering, so values never drift.
- Use `new Date(dateString).toLocaleDateString('en-IN', { weekday: 'short' })` to show day names.
- Template literals and DOM methods are covered on [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org).

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Change the page background colour based on the current condition (sunny, cloudy, rainy).

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Rendered a weather dashboard dynamically from JavaScript data objects
Built a Celsius/Fahrenheit toggle with reusable helper functions
Separated data from display to prepare the app for a live API

3.title: Live Weather from the Open-Meteo API
deliverables: City search that shows real current weather and a 7-day forecast
Loading, not-found and network-error messages
Weather-code to emoji mapping
A demo video searching 2-3 different cities
3.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 2 work — keep working in the same repo.

Connect the dashboard to real weather data using the free Open-Meteo API, which needs no API key. Users can search any city and see its current weather and 7-day forecast, with proper loading and error messages.

**Level:** Intermediate · **Estimated time:** 10-12 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Calling a public REST API with `fetch` and `async`/`await`
- Chaining two API calls (city name to coordinates, then coordinates to weather)
- Reading JSON responses and mapping them to your own data shape
- Handling loading, empty results and network errors

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Try the geocoding API in your browser first: `https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=Pune&count=1`, and find `latitude` and `longitude` in the result.
2. Try the forecast API with those values: `https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=18.52&longitude=73.86&current=temperature_2m,weather_code,wind_speed_10m,relative_humidity_2m&daily=weather_code,temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&timezone=auto`.
3. Write `async function getCoordinates(city)` and `async function getWeather(lat, lon)` that each check `response.ok` and return JSON.
4. Convert the API response into the same shape as your `sampleWeather` object so your Week 2 render functions keep working.
5. Update `getWeatherEmoji` to use Open-Meteo `weather_code` numbers (for example 0 is clear sky, 61-65 is rain).
6. Show a 'Loading...' state during the requests, and show 'City not found' when the geocoding result has no matches.
7. Wrap everything in `try`/`catch` and show a friendly network error, then test with a real city, a fake city and Wi-Fi turned off.

### ✅ Done When
- [ ] Searching a real city shows its actual current temperature and 7 forecast days
- [ ] Searching a made-up city shows a 'City not found' message
- [ ] A loading message appears while data is being fetched
- [ ] A network failure shows an error message instead of a blank or broken page
- [ ] The °C/°F toggle still works with live data

### 💡 Hints & Resources
- If a city returns no `results` field at all, treat it the same as 'not found'.
- Log the raw JSON with `console.log` first so you can see the exact field names before writing render code.
- Disable the Search button while loading to stop users sending many requests at once.
- Full parameter lists are on the [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com) website.

### 🚀 Stretch Goal (optional)
Add a 'Use my location' button with `navigator.geolocation` that skips the geocoding step.

### 📤 Submission
Push your code to GitHub with a short README, then share a LinkedIn post with a 30–60 second demo video or 2–3 screenshots and submit the post link on your dashboard.
post_highlights: Integrated the free Open-Meteo API to show live weather for any city
Chained two API calls with async/await to turn a city name into a forecast
Handled loading, not-found and network errors for a smooth user experience

deliverables: Saved city chips that persist after a refresh

4.description:
### 🎯 This Week's Goal
This week builds on your Week 3 work — keep working in the same repo.

Let users save favourite cities that load with one click and are remembered with localStorage, then polish the app for mobile and accessibility and deploy it. You will finish with a live, useful app you can share.

**Level:** Intermediate+ · **Estimated time:** 10-14 hours

### 📚 What You'll Learn
- Persisting a list of favourites with `localStorage`
- Preventing duplicates and managing a small list in JavaScript
- Responsive design with media queries
- Deploying a static site to GitHub Pages or Netlify

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step
1. Add a 'Save city' button next to the current city name, and store saved cities (name, latitude, longitude) in an array.
2. Save the array to `localStorage` on every change and load it when the page opens.
3. Show saved cities as clickable chips that load that city's weather directly using the stored coordinates.
4. Add a small remove button on each chip and prevent saving the same city twice.
5. Remember the last searched city and the chosen unit so the app opens where the user left off.
6. Add media queries so the dashboard looks good at 375px, and check keyboard access and focus styles.
7. Write a `README.md` with a screenshot, live link and features, then deploy to GitHub Pages or Netlify and test on your phone.

### ✅ Done When
